title: Corporate and Other Laws (Inter P2)
description: Companies Act 2013 (incorporation to audit), the LLP Act 2008 and the Other Laws block (General Clauses Act, Interpretation of Statutes, FEMA) for CA Intermediate Paper 2 under the ICAI new scheme.

chapters.title: Companies Act 2013: Preliminary and Incorporation
chapters.summary: Key definitions (private, public, OPC, small, holding, associate), formation of a company, MOA and AOA, and the doctrines that shape corporate personality.
chapters.lawAsOf: Companies Act 2013 and rules as amended up to November 2026, including G.S.R. 880(E) dated 1 December 2025 (small company limits). Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill 2026 not yet enacted.

lesson.heading: Types of companies you must define precisely
lesson.body:
Most "decide with reasons" questions start with a definition. Learn the conditions as a checklist.

| Type | Section | Conditions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Private company | 2(68) | Articles restrict transfer of shares, limit members to 200 (OPC: 1) and prohibit any invitation to the public to subscribe for securities |
| Public company | 2(71) | Not a private company. A private company that is a subsidiary of a public company is deemed public |
| One Person Company | 2(62) | Only one member. Only a natural person who is an Indian citizen (resident or not) can form or be nominee of an OPC |
| Small company | 2(85) | Not a public company; paid-up capital up to ₹10 crore AND turnover of the preceding financial year up to ₹100 crore |
| Holding / subsidiary | 2(46), 2(87) | Holding company controls the composition of the Board or exercises or controls more than one-half of the total voting power (alone or with its subsidiaries) |
| Associate | 2(6) | Significant influence, meaning control of at least 20% of total voting power or of business decisions under an agreement |
| Government company | 2(45) | At least 51% of paid-up share capital held by the Central Government, State Government(s) or both |

While counting the 200 members of a private company, exclude present employees who are members and former employees who became members while in employment and continue after leaving. Joint holders count as one member.

Small company exclusions: a holding company, a subsidiary company, a section 8 company and a company governed by a special Act cannot be a small company even if it meets both limits. The limits of ₹10 crore and ₹100 crore apply from 1 December 2025 (earlier ₹4 crore and ₹40 crore).

lesson.heading: Formation and incorporation
lesson.body:
Section 3 lets a company be formed for a lawful purpose by:

- 7 or more persons for a public company
- 2 or more persons for a private company
- 1 person for an OPC

Section 3A: if the number of members of a company falls below the minimum and the company carries on business for more than six months, every member who knows of this is severally liable for the debts contracted after those six months.

Incorporation (section 7) is through the SPICe+ web form with the MOA, AOA, a declaration by a professional engaged in the formation (advocate, CA, CMA or CS) and declarations by subscribers and first directors. The Registrar issues a certificate of incorporation with a Corporate Identity Number. Under section 7(2) the certificate is conclusive evidence that all requirements of registration were complied with.

Section 10A: a company with share capital cannot commence business or exercise borrowing powers until a director files a declaration (INC-20A) within 180 days of incorporation that every subscriber has paid for the shares agreed to be taken. Section 12 requires a registered office within 30 days of incorporation.

lesson.heading: Memorandum and articles
lesson.body:
| Point | MOA (section 4) | AOA (section 5) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nature | Charter: defines scope and powers | Internal rules for management |
| Clauses / content | Name, registered office (state), objects, liability, capital, subscription (OPC: nominee) | Regulations for management; Table F to J of Schedule I as models |
| Alteration | Special resolution, plus approval where required (section 13) | Special resolution (section 14) |
| Acts beyond it | Ultra vires the company: void | Ultra vires the articles: can be ratified by altering the articles |

Alteration of MOA under section 13:

- Change of name: special resolution and approval of the Central Government (delegated to the Registrar)
- Shift of registered office from one state to another: special resolution and approval of the Central Government (Regional Director)
- Shift within the same state but to another ROC jurisdiction: confirmation by the Regional Director (section 12(5)); this is not an alteration of the MOA

Entrenchment (section 5(3)): specified articles can be altered only if conditions more restrictive than a special resolution are met. A private company needs the agreement of all members to include them; a public company needs a special resolution. Section 10 makes the MOA and AOA bind the company and members as if each member had signed them.

lesson.heading: Doctrines and the corporate veil
lesson.body:
- **Separate legal entity**: Salomon v Salomon & Co. Ltd (1897). A company is distinct from its members even if one person holds almost all shares.
- **Ultra vires**: Ashbury Railway Carriage and Iron Co. Ltd v Riche (1875). An act beyond the objects in the MOA is void and cannot be ratified even by all members.
- **Constructive notice**: outsiders are deemed to know the contents of the MOA and AOA, which are public documents.
- **Indoor management**: Royal British Bank v Turquand (1856). Outsiders acting in good faith can assume internal formalities were complied with. Exceptions: actual knowledge of the irregularity, suspicion or negligence, forgery, and an outsider who did not read the articles and so cannot claim reliance on them.

Lifting the corporate veil means the court looks behind the company at the persons in control.

| Statutory instances | Judicial instances |
| --- | --- |
| Section 3A (members below minimum) | Fraud or improper conduct (Gilford Motor Co. v Horne, 1933) |
| Section 339 (fraudulent conduct of business in winding up) | Determining enemy character (Daimler Co. v Continental Tyre and Rubber Co., 1916) |
| Misrepresentation in prospectus (sections 34, 35) | Evasion of tax or welfare legislation |
| Section 7(7) (incorporation by false information) | Company used as a sham or agent of its controller |

**Common mistakes**: calling a subsidiary private company a small company; counting employees in the 200-member limit; treating OPC as allowed for foreigners.

keyPoints: Formation: public 7, private 2, OPC 1 member (section 3); section 3A personal liability after 6 months below minimum.
Small company (2(85)): paid-up up to ₹10 crore AND preceding-year turnover up to ₹100 crore from 1 December 2025; holding, subsidiary, section 8 and special-Act companies excluded.
Private company member limit 200 excludes present and certain former employees; joint holders count as one.
Associate = significant influence = at least 20% of total voting power (2(6)).
Certificate of incorporation is conclusive evidence (7(2)); INC-20A declaration within 180 days (10A).
Ultra vires the MOA is void and cannot be ratified (Ashbury v Riche); indoor management protects good-faith outsiders (Turquand).

cases.title: Case: Veda Agritech Private Limited
cases.body:
Veda Agritech Private Limited was incorporated in 2019 with its registered office in Pune, Maharashtra. Kaveri Holdings Private Limited holds 60% of its equity shares. Kaveri Holdings has paid-up capital of ₹1 crore and turnover of ₹6 crore.

| Particulars of Veda (as at 31 March 2026) | Figure |
| --- | --- |
| Paid-up equity share capital | ₹8 crore |
| Turnover for FY 2025-26 | ₹96 crore |
| Members on the register | 190 |
| Of whom: present employees | 14 |
| Of whom: former employees who got shares while employed | 3 |
| Joint holding of Mr and Mrs Rao | 1 folio (counted once in 190) |

The Board proposes (a) to allot shares to 25 outside investors through a private placement and (b) to shift the registered office from Pune to Bengaluru, Karnataka.

questions.prompt: Is Veda Agritech Private Limited a small company for FY 2026-27?
options: No, because it is a subsidiary of Kaveri Holdings
Yes, because paid-up capital and turnover are within the limits
No, because turnover exceeds ₹40 crore
Yes, because a private company is always a small company
questions.explanation: Both figures are within the ₹10 crore and ₹100 crore limits in force from 1 December 2025, but section 2(85) excludes a holding or subsidiary company. Kaveri holds 60%, more than one-half of the voting power, so Veda is a subsidiary and cannot be a small company.

questions.prompt: After the proposed allotment to 25 outside investors, how many members will count towards the 200-member limit of section 2(68)?
questions.explanation: Present employees (14) and former employees who got shares while employed (3) are excluded: 190 - 17 = 173. Joint holders already count as one. 173 + 25 = 198, which is within 200, so the private company status is not affected.

questions.prompt: What approval does Veda need to shift its registered office from Pune to Bengaluru?
options: Special resolution and approval of the Central Government (Regional Director)
Board resolution and intimation to the Registrar within 15 days
Ordinary resolution and approval of the Registrar of Karnataka
Special resolution and approval of the Tribunal only
questions.explanation: Shifting the registered office from one state to another alters the MOA (situation clause). Section 13(4) requires a special resolution and approval of the Central Government, delegated to the Regional Director.

questions.prompt: Kaveri Holdings has paid-up capital of ₹1 crore and turnover of ₹6 crore. Is it a small company?
options: No, because a holding company is excluded from the definition
Yes, because both figures are far below the limits
Yes, if it passes a special resolution to be treated as one
No, because a holding company must have paid-up capital above ₹10 crore
questions.explanation: Section 2(85) excludes both holding and subsidiary companies. Kaveri controls more than one-half of Veda's voting power, so it is a holding company and cannot be a small company whatever its size.

questions.prompt: What is the minimum number of persons required to form a public company under section 3?
questions.explanation: Section 3(1): seven or more persons for a public company, two or more for a private company and one for an OPC.

questions.prompt: Who can incorporate a One Person Company?
options: A natural person who is an Indian citizen, whether resident in India or not
Any natural person resident in India, including a foreign citizen
A natural person or a body corporate
Only an Indian citizen who has stayed in India for at least 182 days
questions.explanation: Under the Companies (Incorporation) Rules as amended in 2021, only a natural person who is an Indian citizen, whether resident in India or otherwise, can form an OPC or be its nominee. A body corporate cannot.

questions.prompt: A company holds 22% of the total voting power of B Ltd but does not control its Board. B Ltd is its:
options: Associate company
Subsidiary company
Holding company
Joint venture by default
questions.explanation: Section 2(6) treats control of at least 20% of total voting power as significant influence, making B Ltd an associate. More than one-half of voting power or control of Board composition would be needed for a subsidiary.

questions.prompt: An act that is ultra vires the memorandum can be ratified if all the members agree to it in a general meeting.
questions.explanation: In Ashbury Railway Carriage and Iron Co. Ltd v Riche the House of Lords held that an act beyond the objects clause is void ab initio. Even unanimous consent of members cannot ratify it. Acts ultra vires only the articles or the directors can be ratified.

questions.prompt: Under section 7(2), the certificate of incorporation issued by the Registrar is conclusive evidence that all requirements of registration have been complied with.
questions.explanation: Section 7(2) makes the certificate conclusive evidence. If incorporation was obtained by false information, the remedy lies under section 7(7) before the Tribunal, not by challenging the certificate as invalid.

questions.prompt: Which of these companies can NEVER be a small company, whatever their capital and turnover? Select all that apply.
options: A section 8 company
A subsidiary company
A company governed by a special Act
A One Person Company
A private company with paid-up capital of ₹9 crore
questions.explanation: The proviso to section 2(85) excludes holding and subsidiary companies, section 8 companies and companies governed by a special Act. An OPC is a private company and can be small if within the limits.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: the doctrine of indoor management was laid down in Royal British Bank v ___.
questions.explanation: Royal British Bank v Turquand (1856): an outsider dealing in good faith may assume that internal procedures required by the articles have been complied with.

questions.prompt: Explain the circumstances in which the corporate veil may be lifted, giving statutory and judicial instances.
questions.answer:
A company is a separate legal person (Salomon v Salomon & Co., 1897), but courts and the Act ignore that separation where it is abused.

Statutory instances:
- Section 3A: members fall below the minimum for more than six months; members aware of it are severally liable.
- Sections 34 and 35: misstatement in prospectus.
- Section 339: fraudulent conduct of business found in winding up.
- Section 7(7): incorporation obtained by furnishing false information.

Judicial instances:
- Fraud or evasion of obligations, for example Gilford Motor Co. v Horne (1933), where a company was formed to evade a restrictive covenant.
- Determining enemy character, Daimler Co. v Continental Tyre and Rubber Co. (1916).
- Evasion of tax or welfare laws, and a company used as a sham or agent of its controllers.

questions.prompt: Decide with reasons: Pragati Ltd, a public company, had 7 members. Two members died in April 2025 and their shares were not transmitted. The company kept trading with 5 members. In February 2026 a supplier, owed ₹6 lakh for goods supplied in January 2026, sues Mr Iyer, a member who knew the membership had fallen. Is Mr Iyer liable?
questions.answer:
Provision: section 3A. If a company carries on business for more than six months while the number of members is below the minimum (7 for a public company), every person who is a member during that time and knows of it is severally liable for the payment of the whole debts contracted after those six months, and can be sued for them.

Analysis: membership fell to 5 in April 2025. Six months expired in October 2025. The debt of ₹6 lakh was contracted in January 2026, after the six-month period. Mr Iyer was a member and aware of the shortfall.

Conclusion: Mr Iyer is severally liable for the ₹6 lakh. The supplier can sue him without suing the company or other members. This is a statutory case of lifting the corporate veil.

questions.prompt: Explain the doctrine of constructive notice and the doctrine of indoor management. State the exceptions to indoor management.
questions.answer:
Constructive notice: the MOA and AOA are registered with the Registrar and are public documents. Every person dealing with the company is deemed to know their contents. An outsider cannot plead ignorance of a limit on a director's authority that appears in the articles.

Indoor management (Royal British Bank v Turquand): the outsider is not bound to inquire into internal proceedings. If the articles permit an act subject to an internal formality (such as a resolution), the outsider acting in good faith can assume the formality was completed.

Exceptions: (a) actual or constructive knowledge of the irregularity; (b) suspicion of irregularity or negligence in not inquiring; (c) forgery, which makes the act void; (d) an act outside the apparent authority of the officer; (e) an outsider who never read the articles cannot claim he relied on them.

questions.prompt: What does section 10A require before a company with share capital can commence business, and what follows if it is not complied with?
questions.answer:
Section 10A applies to a company with share capital incorporated after the Companies (Amendment) Ordinance, 2018 (from 2 November 2018).

- A director must file a declaration (Form INC-20A) with the Registrar within 180 days of incorporation stating that every subscriber to the MOA has paid the value of the shares agreed to be taken.
- Until this is filed, the company cannot commence business or exercise borrowing powers.
- Default attracts a penalty on the company and on every officer in default.
- If the declaration is not filed within 180 days and the Registrar has reasonable cause to believe the company is not carrying on business, he may initiate removal of its name from the register under Chapter XVIII.

chapters.title: Prospectus and Allotment of Securities
chapters.summary: How securities reach investors: public offer by prospectus, shelf and red herring prospectus, liability for misstatements, allotment rules and private placement under section 42.
chapters.lawAsOf: Companies Act 2013 sections 23-42 and Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules 2014 as amended up to November 2026. Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill 2026 not yet enacted.

lesson.heading: Modes of issue and kinds of prospectus
lesson.body:
Section 23 sets out who can issue securities and how:

| Company | Permitted modes |
| --- | --- |
| Public company | Public offer through prospectus; private placement; rights issue; bonus issue |
| Private company | Private placement; rights issue; bonus issue (no public offer) |

A prospectus (section 2(70)) is any document described or issued as a prospectus, including a red herring prospectus, a shelf prospectus, and any notice, circular or advertisement inviting offers from the public.

| Kind | Section | Key feature |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Deemed prospectus | 25 | Company allots securities to an intermediary (issuing house) for offer to the public. The offer document is deemed a prospectus if the public offer is made within 6 months after allotment, or before the company receives the whole consideration |
| Shelf prospectus | 31 | Classes of companies notified by SEBI; one prospectus for several issues over a validity period of 1 year from the opening of the first offer; an information memorandum is filed before each later offer |
| Red herring prospectus | 32 | Issued before the price or quantity is fixed; filed with the ROC before the issue opens; the final prospectus with price and quantity is filed after the offer closes |
| Abridged prospectus | 33 | Memorandum of salient features; must accompany every application form |

Section 26 requires the prospectus to be dated, signed and filed with the Registrar on or before the date of publication. It cannot be issued more than 90 days after it is filed.

lesson.heading: Liability for misstatement in prospectus
lesson.body:
| Point | Criminal liability (section 34) | Civil liability (section 35) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Who | Every person who authorises the issue | Directors, persons named as directors with consent, promoters, persons who authorised the issue, experts |
| Remedy | Punishment under section 447 (fraud) | Compensation to every person who subscribed on the faith of the prospectus and suffered loss |
| Defence | Statement was immaterial, or the person had reasonable grounds to believe and did believe it was true | Withdrew consent before issue and it was issued without authority; or it was issued without knowledge or consent and he gave reasonable public notice on becoming aware |

Under section 35(3), where the prospectus was issued with intent to defraud, every person who knowingly was a party is personally liable without limitation of liability.

Section 36 punishes fraudulently inducing a person to invest money, and section 38 punishes personation (applying in a fictitious name or making multiple applications in different names). Both attract section 447.

lesson.heading: Allotment of securities (sections 39 and 40)
lesson.body:
- No allotment unless the minimum subscription stated in the prospectus has been subscribed and the sums payable on application received (section 39(1)).
- Application money must be at least 5% of the nominal amount of the security or such other percentage as SEBI specifies (section 39(2)).
- If the minimum subscription is not received within 30 days of issue of the prospectus (or the period SEBI specifies), the money must be repaid. Under rule 11, repayment is due within 15 days from closure of the issue; otherwise the directors who are officers in default are jointly and severally liable to repay with interest at 15% per annum.
- Return of allotment in Form PAS-3 to the Registrar (section 39(4)).
- Section 40: before a public offer the company must apply to one or more recognised stock exchanges for listing. Application money is kept in a separate bank account with a scheduled bank and used only for adjustment against allotment or for repayment.
- Underwriting commission (rule 13) cannot exceed 5% of the issue price of shares or 2% of the issue price of debentures, or the rate in the articles, whichever is lower.

lesson.heading: Private placement (section 42) and worked example
lesson.body:
Private placement means an offer of securities to a select group of persons, other than by public offer, through a private placement offer cum application letter (Form PAS-4).

| Condition | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| Number of persons | Not more than 200 in a financial year, counted separately for each kind of security, excluding qualified institutional buyers and employees offered securities under an ESOP |
| Approval | Special resolution for each offer (for non-convertible debentures, one special resolution a year can cover all offers) |
| Minimum investment | Face value of at least ₹20,000 per person |
| Identified persons | Offer only to persons whose names are recorded before the invitation; no public advertisement |
| Payment | From the subscriber's bank account by cheque, demand draft or banking channel; never in cash |
| Allotment | Within 60 days of receipt of application money; else refund within 15 days after the 60 days, failing which interest at 12% per annum from the 60th day |
| Return of allotment | Form PAS-3 within 15 days of allotment |

Worked example: a company offers equity in one financial year to 215 persons, of whom 12 are QIBs and 8 are employees under an ESOP. Persons counted = 215 - 12 - 8 = 195. The offer is within the limit.

If the offer breaches section 42, the company, promoters and directors face a penalty up to the amount raised or ₹2 crore, whichever is lower, and the money must be refunded within 30 days of the penalty order.

**Common mistakes**: counting QIBs in the 200; forgetting that each kind of security has its own 200 limit; accepting cash in a private placement.

keyPoints: Private company: no public offer; only private placement, rights or bonus (section 23).
Deemed prospectus (25): public offer within 6 months of allotment to an intermediary.
Shelf prospectus valid for 1 year from opening of first offer; information memorandum for each later offer (31).
Section 34 criminal (section 447) and section 35 civil liability for untrue statements in prospectus.
Application money at least 5% of nominal value; minimum subscription within 30 days, else refund (39).
Private placement: up to 200 persons per FY per security (excl. QIBs and ESOP employees), ₹20,000 minimum, allot in 60 days, PAS-3 in 15 days (42).

cases.title: Case: Suryodaya Solar Limited
cases.body:
Suryodaya Solar Limited, an unlisted public company, passed a special resolution in May 2026 to raise ₹40 crore through a private placement of equity shares of face value ₹10 each.

| Offer details (FY 2026-27) | Number |
| --- | --- |
| Total persons to whom offer letters were sent | 230 |
| Of whom: qualified institutional buyers | 40 |
| Of whom: employees under the company's ESOP | 10 |

Application money was received on 1 June 2026. One investor, Mr Bansal, paid ₹25 lakh in cash at the registered office. The company placed the money in its regular current account. Because of a valuation dispute, allotment was still pending on 10 August 2026.

questions.prompt: How many persons count towards the 200-person limit for this private placement?
questions.explanation: QIBs and employees offered securities under an ESOP are excluded from the 200 limit in section 42. 230 - 40 - 10 = 180, which is within the limit.

questions.prompt: Allotment was not made within 60 days of 1 June 2026. What is the company's obligation?
options: Repay the application money within 15 days after the 60 days expire; if it fails, repay with interest at 12% per annum from the 60th day
Repay within 30 days with interest at 15% per annum
Nothing, as long as allotment is made within 90 days
Treat the money as a deposit and file DPT-3
questions.explanation: Section 42: allotment must be made within 60 days of receipt of application money. Otherwise the money is repaid within 15 days from the expiry of the 60 days. If not repaid in that time, it is repayable with interest at 12% per annum from the 60th day.

questions.prompt: What is the legal position on Mr Bansal's cash payment and on keeping the money in the regular current account?
options: Both are contraventions: payment must come from the subscriber's bank account, and money must be kept in a separate bank account
Cash is allowed up to ₹50 lakh; the account used does not matter
Cash is a contravention, but the current account is fine
Both are allowed for an unlisted company
questions.explanation: Section 42 requires payment by cheque, demand draft or other banking channel, not cash, and requires the application money to be kept in a separate bank account, used only for adjustment against allotment or repayment.

questions.prompt: When Suryodaya finally allots the shares, within how many days must it file the return of allotment in Form PAS-3?
options: 15 days
30 days
60 days
7 days
questions.explanation: Section 42 requires the return of allotment for a private placement to be filed within 15 days of allotment. Default attracts a penalty on the company, promoters and directors.

questions.prompt: A shelf prospectus is valid for:
options: One year from the date of opening of the first offer
Six months from the date of filing
Three years from the date of filing
Until all securities under it are issued
questions.explanation: Section 31(1): the shelf prospectus has a validity of one year from the opening of the first offer. No further prospectus is needed for later offers in that period, only an information memorandum.

questions.prompt: A company allots shares to an issuing house, which offers them to the public 4 months later. The offer document is:
options: A deemed prospectus under section 25, with the company liable as if it issued a prospectus
An information memorandum
Not a prospectus because the company did not offer the shares itself
A private placement offer letter
questions.explanation: Section 25: when the public offer is made within 6 months after allotment, the document is deemed a prospectus issued by the company, and all liability for misstatement applies.

questions.prompt: The maximum underwriting commission on an issue of shares under rule 13 is:
options: 5% of the issue price, or the rate in the articles, whichever is lower
2% of the issue price
10% of the issue price
Any rate approved by special resolution
questions.explanation: Commission on shares cannot exceed 5% of the issue price, and on debentures 2%, or the rate authorised by the articles, whichever is less.

questions.prompt: A private company with more than ₹50 crore paid-up capital may issue a prospectus inviting the public to subscribe for its shares.
questions.explanation: A private company's articles must prohibit any invitation to the public (section 2(68)) and section 23(2) limits it to private placement, rights or bonus issue, whatever its size.

questions.prompt: In a public issue, the amount payable on application on each security must be at least 5% of its nominal amount, unless SEBI specifies otherwise.
questions.explanation: Section 39(2) sets the floor at 5% of the nominal amount or such other percentage or amount as SEBI may specify.

questions.prompt: Which of these are valid defences for a director against civil liability under section 35 for an untrue statement in the prospectus? Select all that apply.
options: He withdrew his consent to be a director before the prospectus was issued and it was issued without his authority
The prospectus was issued without his knowledge or consent and, on becoming aware, he gave reasonable public notice of it
He did not attend the Board meeting that approved the prospectus
He had been a director for only two months
questions.explanation: Section 35(2) protects a person who withdrew consent before issue or who did not know of the issue and gave reasonable public notice. Absence from a meeting or a short tenure is not a defence.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: a prospectus that does not include complete particulars of the quantum or price of securities is called a ___ prospectus.
questions.explanation: Section 32 explanation: a red herring prospectus omits price or quantity. After the offer closes, the final prospectus with these details is filed with the Registrar and SEBI.

questions.prompt: State the conditions that a company must satisfy to make a private placement under section 42.
questions.answer:
- Offer only to identified persons whose names are recorded before the invitation, through a private placement offer cum application letter (PAS-4).
- Not more than 200 persons in a financial year, for each kind of security, excluding QIBs and employees under an ESOP.
- Prior special resolution of members for each offer (for NCDs, one special resolution a year).
- Minimum investment size of ₹20,000 of face value per person.
- Payment only through banking channels from the subscriber's account, not cash; money kept in a separate bank account.
- No public advertisement or use of media or marketing networks.
- Allotment within 60 days of receipt of application money, else refund within the next 15 days, failing which interest at 12% per annum from the 60th day.
- No fresh offer while an earlier offer is pending allotment.
- Return of allotment (PAS-3) within 15 days of allotment.
- Contravention: penalty up to the amount involved or ₹2 crore, whichever is lower, and refund within 30 days of the penalty order.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between criminal liability under section 34 and civil liability under section 35 for misstatements in a prospectus.
questions.answer:
- Nature: section 34 is punishment for the offence; section 35 provides compensation to investors.
- Persons liable: section 34 covers every person who authorises the issue. Section 35 covers the company, every director at the time of issue, persons named as directors with consent, promoters, persons authorising the issue and experts.
- Consequence: section 34 attracts punishment under section 447 (imprisonment from 6 months to 10 years and fine). Section 35 makes the persons liable to pay compensation to subscribers who suffered loss.
- Defence: under section 34, the statement was immaterial or the person had reasonable grounds to believe it true. Under section 35(2), withdrawal of consent before issue, or issue without knowledge and prompt public notice.
- Under section 35(3), if the issue was made with intent to defraud, every person who knowingly was a party is personally liable without limitation of liability.

questions.prompt: Decide with reasons: Arohi Ltd issued a prospectus stating that its factory 'has all environmental clearances'. One clearance had expired 3 months earlier. Mr Shetty, a director, says he relied on the CFO's note and believed the statement. Investor Ms Kapoor, who bought shares in the issue, lost ₹4 lakh when the factory was sealed. Discuss Mr Shetty's criminal and civil liability.
questions.answer:
Provisions: section 34 (criminal liability) and section 35 (civil liability) for untrue or misleading statements in a prospectus.

Criminal liability: section 34 gives a defence if the person proves he had reasonable grounds to believe, and did up to the time of issue believe, that the statement was true. If Mr Shetty can show the CFO's note was a reasonable basis (for example, the note was recent and specific), he may escape punishment under section 447. Mere belief without reasonable grounds is not enough.

Civil liability: under section 35 every director at the time of issue is liable to compensate persons who subscribed on the faith of the prospectus and suffered loss. The section 35(2) defences are limited to withdrawal of consent before issue or issue without knowledge with prompt public notice. Neither applies, as Mr Shetty approved the prospectus.

Conclusion: Mr Shetty is liable to compensate Ms Kapoor for her loss of ₹4 lakh. His criminal liability depends on proving reasonable grounds for belief.

questions.prompt: Explain the shelf prospectus and the red herring prospectus, and how they differ.
questions.answer:
Shelf prospectus (section 31): issued by classes of companies notified by SEBI for one or more issues of securities over a period. It is valid for one year from the opening of the first offer. For each subsequent offer, the company files an information memorandum with material changes (new charges, changes in financial position) since the previous offer; no fresh prospectus is needed.

Red herring prospectus (section 32): used in book building. It does not contain complete particulars of the price or quantity of securities. It is filed with the Registrar at least three days before the issue opens and carries the same obligations as a prospectus. Any variation between it and the final prospectus is highlighted. After the offer closes, the final prospectus with price and quantity is filed with the Registrar and SEBI.

Difference: a shelf prospectus covers a series of issues over a year; a red herring prospectus covers one issue where price or quantity is still to be discovered.

chapters.title: Share Capital and Debentures
chapters.summary: Kinds of share capital, securities premium, sweat equity, rights and bonus issues, buy-back, transfer of shares and the rules for issuing debentures.
chapters.lawAsOf: Companies Act 2013 sections 43-72 and Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules 2014 as amended up to November 2026. Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill 2026 not yet enacted.

lesson.heading: Kinds of capital and issue price rules
lesson.body:
Section 43: share capital of a company limited by shares is of two kinds.

- **Equity share capital**: with voting rights, or with differential rights as to dividend, voting or otherwise (as per the rules).
- **Preference share capital**: carries a preferential right to dividend (fixed amount or rate) and to repayment of capital in winding up.

| Provision | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Section 52 Securities premium | Premium goes to a securities premium account; usable only for: issuing fully paid bonus shares, writing off preliminary expenses, writing off expenses, commission or discount on issue of shares or debentures, premium on redemption of preference shares or debentures, and buy-back (section 68) |
| Section 53 Discount | Issue of shares at a discount is void, except sweat equity shares (and shares issued to creditors under a debt restructuring scheme). Penalty: amount raised at discount or ₹5 lakh, whichever is less, and refund with 12% interest |
| Section 54 Sweat equity | Issued to directors or employees for know-how or value additions. Special resolution; yearly limit 15% of existing paid-up equity capital or issue value of ₹5 crore, whichever is higher; total not more than 25% of paid-up equity capital (50% for a start-up within 10 years of incorporation); lock-in of 3 years |
| Section 55 Preference shares | No irredeemable preference shares. Redeemable within 20 years (up to 30 years for infrastructure projects, with at least 10% redeemed each year from the 21st year). Redemption only out of profits available for dividend or a fresh issue; when out of profits, an equal amount goes to the capital redemption reserve |

lesson.heading: Further issue: rights, ESOP, preferential and bonus
lesson.body:
Section 62 governs further issue of share capital:

- **Rights issue (62(1)(a))**: offer to existing equity holders in proportion to their holding, open for not less than 15 days and not more than 30 days (a private company may fix a shorter period if 90% of its members consent). The offer includes a right to renounce in favour of others unless the articles say otherwise. Unsubscribed shares may be disposed of by the Board in a manner not disadvantageous to shareholders and the company.
- **ESOP (62(1)(b))**: to employees by special resolution.
- **Preferential allotment (62(1)(c))**: to any persons, for cash or other consideration, by special resolution, with the price determined by a registered valuer.

**Bonus shares (section 63)** can be issued only out of free reserves, securities premium account or capital redemption reserve, and never out of revaluation reserve. Conditions: authorised by articles; recommended by the Board and approved in general meeting; no default in payment of interest or principal on fixed deposits or debt securities; no default in statutory dues of employees; partly paid shares made fully paid. Bonus shares cannot be issued in lieu of dividend. Once announced, the decision cannot be withdrawn.

lesson.heading: Buy-back (sections 68-70) with worked example
lesson.body:
Sources: free reserves, securities premium account, or proceeds of an earlier issue of shares or other specified securities (but not the proceeds of an earlier issue of the same kind).

Conditions under section 68:

- Authorised by the articles.
- Special resolution, except where the buy-back is 10% or less of total paid-up equity capital and free reserves; then a Board resolution is enough.
- Buy-back not more than 25% of aggregate paid-up capital and free reserves; for equity shares, not more than 25% of total paid-up equity capital in that financial year.
- Debt-equity ratio after buy-back: secured and unsecured debts not more than twice paid-up capital and free reserves.
- Shares fully paid; completed within one year of the resolution; no fresh buy-back offer within one year from closure of the preceding offer.
- Declaration of solvency filed with the Registrar; shares extinguished within 7 days of completion; no further issue of the same kind for 6 months except bonus or conversion.
- Section 70 bars buy-back through a subsidiary or investment company, or while a default in repaying deposits or term loans subsists.

For section 68, "free reserves" includes the securities premium account.

Worked example:

| Particulars | ₹ crore |
| --- | --- |
| Paid-up equity capital | 40.00 |
| General reserve (free) | 24.00 |
| Securities premium | 6.00 |
| **Paid-up capital and free reserves** | **70.00** |
| Board limit (10%) | 7.00 |
| Special resolution limit (25%) | 17.50 |

lesson.heading: Transfer of shares and debentures
lesson.body:
- **Section 56**: the instrument of transfer, duly stamped and executed by transferor and transferee, must be delivered to the company within 60 days of execution. Certificates are delivered within 1 month of receipt of the instrument (2 months of incorporation for subscribers).
- **Section 58**: a private company refusing registration must send notice of refusal within 30 days of receipt of the instrument; the transferee may appeal to the Tribunal within 30 days of the notice, or within 60 days of delivery if no notice is sent. For a public company, shares are freely transferable; on refusal, an appeal lies within 60 days of refusal notice or 90 days of delivery if no notice.

Debentures (section 71):

- Can be issued with an option to convert into shares, wholly or partly, with approval by special resolution.
- Debentures carrying voting rights cannot be issued.
- Secured debentures (rule 18): tenure up to 10 years (longer for specified infrastructure sectors), secured by a charge on assets, and a debenture trustee must be appointed where the offer is to the public or to more than 500 persons.
- Debenture redemption reserve and investment of a portion of debentures maturing in the year are required for specified classes of companies under rule 18(7); listed companies are exempt from DRR after the 2019 amendment.

**Common mistakes**: using revaluation reserve for bonus; forgetting that securities premium counts as free reserve only for buy-back; using a board resolution for a buy-back above 10%.

keyPoints: Securities premium: 5 permitted uses only (section 52); never for dividend.
Issue at discount is void except sweat equity (section 53).
Sweat equity: 15% of paid-up equity or ₹5 crore a year (higher), cap 25% (start-up 50% for 10 years).
No irredeemable preference shares; maximum 20 years (infrastructure 30) (section 55).
Bonus only from free reserves, securities premium or CRR; never revaluation reserve; not in lieu of dividend.
Buy-back: Board up to 10%, special resolution up to 25% of paid-up capital and free reserves; debt-equity 2:1; one-year gap.
Debentures cannot carry voting rights (71(2)); debenture trustee if issue to public or more than 500 persons.

cases.title: Case: Meridian Textiles Limited
cases.body:
Meridian Textiles Limited, an unlisted public company incorporated in 2015, has these balances as per its latest audited balance sheet:

| Particulars | ₹ crore |
| --- | --- |
| Equity share capital (5 crore shares of ₹10, fully paid) | 50.00 |
| General reserve | 30.00 |
| Securities premium | 10.00 |
| Revaluation reserve | 15.00 |
| Secured and unsecured loans | 120.00 |

Its articles authorise buy-back and bonus issues. Its last buy-back offer closed on 20 September 2025. In August 2026 the Board proposes:

- a fresh buy-back approved only by a Board resolution;
- a bonus issue funded from the revaluation reserve;
- sweat equity shares to the chief technology officer for a patented process.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum amount Meridian can spend on a buy-back approved by a Board resolution alone? Answer in ₹ crore to 2 decimals.
questions.explanation:
Proviso to section 68(2)(b): a Board resolution suffices if the buy-back is 10% or less of total paid-up equity capital and free reserves. Free reserves include the securities premium account for this section. Revaluation reserve is not a free reserve.

| Particulars | ₹ crore |
| --- | --- |
| Paid-up equity capital | 50.00 |
| General reserve | 30.00 |
| Securities premium | 10.00 |
| **Total** | **90.00** |
| 10% | **9.00** |

questions.prompt: Can Meridian make the new buy-back offer in August 2026?
options: No, a buy-back offer cannot be made within one year from the closure of the preceding offer
Yes, because the earlier buy-back was in a different financial year
Yes, if a special resolution is passed instead of a Board resolution
No, because an unlisted company cannot buy back its shares
questions.explanation: Section 68(2) bars a fresh buy-back offer within one year from the date of closure of the preceding offer. The last offer closed on 20 September 2025, so no offer is possible before 20 September 2026, whatever the resolution.

questions.prompt: Is the proposed bonus issue from the revaluation reserve valid?
options: No, section 63 prohibits bonus shares out of reserves created by revaluation of assets
Yes, any reserve can be capitalised with members' approval
Yes, if the auditor certifies the revaluation
No, because an unlisted company cannot issue bonus shares
questions.explanation: Section 63(1) allows bonus shares only out of free reserves, securities premium account or capital redemption reserve, and its proviso bars capitalising reserves created by revaluation of assets. Meridian can use the general reserve or securities premium instead.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum sweat equity Meridian can issue in one year under rule 8?
options: 15% of existing paid-up equity capital or shares of issue value ₹5 crore, whichever is higher
25% of existing paid-up equity capital in every year
₹5 crore of issue value, whichever is lower
10% of paid-up capital and free reserves
questions.explanation: Rule 8(4) limits sweat equity in a year to 15% of existing paid-up equity share capital or issue value of ₹5 crore, whichever is higher. Total sweat equity cannot exceed 25% of paid-up equity capital at any time. For Meridian, 15% of ₹50 crore = ₹7.5 crore of paid-up capital.

questions.prompt: The maximum period for which a company (other than for infrastructure projects) can issue redeemable preference shares is:
options: 20 years
10 years
30 years
No limit if the articles permit
questions.explanation: Section 55(2): preference shares must be redeemable within 20 years. For infrastructure projects, up to 30 years with redemption of at least 10% a year from the 21st year.

questions.prompt: A company issues equity shares of ₹10 each at ₹9. The issue is:
options: Void, because shares cannot be issued at a discount except sweat equity
Valid if a special resolution is passed
Valid if the Tribunal approves
Valid for a private company
questions.explanation: Section 53(1) prohibits issue of shares at a discount, and 53(2) declares such shares void, except sweat equity shares and shares issued to creditors under a statutory debt-conversion scheme.

questions.prompt: In a rights issue by a public company, the offer must remain open for:
options: Not less than 15 days and not more than 30 days
Not less than 7 days and not more than 15 days
Exactly 21 days
Not less than 30 days
questions.explanation: Section 62(1)(a)(i): the offer is made by notice specifying the number of shares, limited to a period of not less than 15 days and not exceeding 30 days. A private company may fix a shorter period with the consent of 90% of its members.

questions.prompt: A company may issue debentures carrying voting rights if its articles permit.
questions.explanation: Section 71(2) says no company shall issue debentures carrying any voting rights. Articles cannot override this.

questions.prompt: A company can issue irredeemable preference shares if its articles authorise it.
questions.explanation: Section 55(1) prohibits issue of irredeemable preference shares by any company limited by shares.

questions.prompt: For which purposes can the securities premium account be applied under section 52? Select all that apply.
options: Issue of fully paid bonus shares
Writing off preliminary expenses
Premium payable on redemption of preference shares or debentures
Payment of dividend to equity shareholders
Writing off a trading loss of the year
Buy-back of its own shares
questions.explanation: Section 52(2) permits five uses: bonus shares, preliminary expenses, expenses or commission or discount on issue of shares or debentures, premium on redemption of preference shares or debentures, and buy-back under section 68. Dividend and loss write-off are not permitted.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: under section 56, the instrument of transfer of shares must be delivered to the company within ___ days of its execution.
questions.explanation: Section 56(1): the duly stamped, dated and executed instrument of transfer, with the share certificate, is delivered within 60 days of execution.

questions.prompt: State the conditions for buy-back of securities under section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013.
questions.answer:
- Authorised by the articles.
- Special resolution in general meeting; a Board resolution suffices if the buy-back is 10% or less of total paid-up equity capital and free reserves.
- Buy-back not more than 25% of the aggregate of paid-up capital and free reserves; for equity shares, not more than 25% of paid-up equity capital in a financial year.
- Post buy-back debt (secured and unsecured) not more than twice paid-up capital and free reserves.
- All securities fully paid.
- Sources: free reserves, securities premium or proceeds of a different kind of issue.
- Completed within one year of the resolution; no fresh offer within one year from closure of the preceding offer.
- Declaration of solvency filed; securities extinguished within 7 days; no further issue of the same kind for 6 months except bonus or conversion.
- If out of free reserves or premium, transfer the nominal value to the capital redemption reserve (section 69).
- Section 70: no buy-back through subsidiaries or investment companies or while a default in deposits, debentures or term loans subsists.

questions.prompt: Decide with reasons: Nilgiri Foods Ltd made a rights offer of 10 lakh shares. 2 lakh shares were not taken up. The Board allotted them to Mr Kumar, a close friend of the MD, at the rights price, which was 40% below market value. A shareholder objects. Is the Board's action valid?
questions.answer:
Provision: section 62(1)(a)(iii). After the rights offer period expires, or on receipt of a declination, the Board may dispose of unsubscribed shares in such manner as is not disadvantageous to the shareholders and the company.

Analysis: allotting 2 lakh shares at a price 40% below market value to a person connected with the MD confers a benefit on him at the cost of the company and existing shareholders. Such disposal is disadvantageous to them and is not a fair exercise of the Board's discretion. If the Board wished to issue to a specific outsider at a set price, it should have followed section 62(1)(c) (preferential allotment by special resolution, price based on a registered valuer's report).

Conclusion: the allotment is open to challenge. The objecting shareholder can seek relief, and the allotment is liable to be set aside as an improper exercise of the Board's power.

questions.prompt: When can a private company refuse to register a transfer of shares, and what remedy does the transferee have under section 58?
questions.answer:
- A private company may refuse registration under a power in its articles, since its articles restrict transfer.
- Notice of refusal with reasons must be sent to the transferor and transferee within 30 days of receipt of the instrument of transfer.
- The transferee may appeal to the Tribunal against the refusal within 30 days of receipt of the notice, or, if no notice is sent, within 60 days of the date of delivery of the instrument to the company.
- The Tribunal may dismiss the appeal or direct that the transfer be registered within 10 days of its order, and may order rectification of the register and payment of damages.
- If the company does not comply with the order, the company and officers in default face punishment under section 58(6).

questions.prompt: Explain the conditions for issue of bonus shares under section 63.
questions.answer:
Sources: free reserves, securities premium account or capital redemption reserve. Reserves created by revaluation of assets cannot be capitalised.

Conditions:
- Authorised by the articles.
- Recommended by the Board and authorised in general meeting.
- No default in payment of interest or principal on fixed deposits or debt securities.
- No default in payment of statutory dues of employees such as PF, gratuity and bonus.
- Partly paid shares outstanding must be made fully paid before the issue.
- The company must comply with any conditions prescribed in the rules.

Further points: bonus shares cannot be issued in lieu of dividend. Once the Board announces a bonus issue, it cannot withdraw it.

chapters.title: Acceptance of Deposits by Companies
chapters.summary: What counts as a deposit, the receipts excluded from it, how companies accept deposits from members and the public, and the limits, reserves and returns involved.
chapters.lawAsOf: Companies Act 2013 sections 73-76A and Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules 2014 as amended up to November 2026. Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill 2026 not yet enacted.

lesson.heading: Meaning of deposit and the exclusions
lesson.body:
Section 2(31) defines deposit as any receipt of money by way of deposit or loan or in any other form by a company, except classes of amounts prescribed in consultation with RBI. Rule 2(1)(c) lists those exclusions. The most examined ones:

| Receipt | Not a deposit if |
| --- | --- |
| From Central or State Government, or guaranteed by it | Always excluded |
| Loans from banks, public financial institutions, insurance companies, scheduled banks | Always excluded |
| From any other company | Always excluded |
| Share application money | Securities allotted within 60 days of receipt; if not, refunded within 15 days after the 60 days. Otherwise it becomes a deposit |
| From a director (or, for a private company, a relative of a director) | The person gives a written declaration that the money is not borrowed or received from others |
| Advance for supply of goods or services | Appropriated against the supply within 365 days |
| Security deposit for performance of a contract, or advance for long-term projects | Within the conditions of the rule |
| Unsecured loan from promoters | Brought in under a stipulation of a lending institution, until the loan is repaid |
| Convertible note of a start-up | ₹25 lakh or more in a single tranche, convertible into equity or repayable within 10 years |
| Non-interest-bearing security deposit from an employee | Up to the employee's annual salary |
| Secured bonds or debentures; compulsorily convertible debentures | Within the conditions of the rule |

Section 73(1) does not apply to a banking company, an NBFC registered with RBI, a housing finance company registered with the National Housing Bank, and other notified companies.

lesson.heading: Deposits from members (section 73(2))
lesson.body:
A company may accept deposits from its members by ordinary resolution in general meeting, subject to rules made in consultation with RBI and these conditions:

- Issue a circular to members with a statement of its financial position, credit rating (if any), total deposits accepted and outstanding, and particulars of defaults.
- File a copy of the circular with the Registrar at least 30 days before the date of issue of the circular.
- Deposit, on or before 30 April each year, at least 20% of the deposits maturing in the next financial year in a separate scheduled bank account called the deposit repayment reserve account.
- Certify that there is no default in repayment of earlier deposits or interest.
- Provide security, if the deposit is secured, by creating a charge.

Limits under rule 3:

| Company | Limit (on aggregate of paid-up share capital, free reserves and securities premium) |
| --- | --- |
| Public company accepting from members under 73(2) | 35% |
| Private company accepting from members | 100% |
| Eligible company: from members | 10% |
| Eligible company: other deposits (public) | 25% |
| Government company | 35% |

Tenure: not less than 6 months and not more than 36 months. For short-term needs, deposits for at least 3 months are allowed up to 10% of the same aggregate. Interest and brokerage cannot exceed the maximum rate RBI prescribes for NBFCs.

Private company exemption (MCA notification of 2015, as amended): section 73(2)(a) to (e) does not apply to a private company that accepts from members up to 100% of paid-up capital, free reserves and securities premium; or is a start-up for 10 years from incorporation; or is not an associate or subsidiary of another company, has borrowings from banks, financial institutions or body corporates not more than twice its paid-up capital or ₹50 crore (whichever is lower) and has no default in repaying them. It still files the details with the Registrar.

lesson.heading: Deposits from the public by eligible companies (section 76)
lesson.body:
An eligible company is a public company with net worth of at least ₹100 crore or turnover of at least ₹500 crore that has obtained the prior consent of members by special resolution and filed it with the Registrar before inviting deposits. Additional requirements:

- Advertisement in the form prescribed, in English and vernacular newspapers.
- Credit rating obtained every year and sent to the Registrar with DPT-3.
- For secured deposits, a charge on assets in favour of depositors.
- Limits of 10% (members) and 25% (others), as in the table above.

Returns and records:

- Register of deposits at the registered office, preserved for 8 years from the end of the financial year of the latest entry.
- Return of deposits in Form DPT-3 by 30 June every year, with information as on 31 March, audited by the auditor.

Consequences: section 74 deals with deposits accepted before 1 April 2014. Under section 75, if a company fails to repay deposits that were accepted with intent to defraud, every officer responsible is personally liable without limitation of liability. Section 76A: the company must repay the deposit with interest and is liable to a fine of not less than ₹1 crore or twice the deposit accepted, whichever is lower, up to ₹10 crore; and every officer in default to imprisonment up to 7 years and a fine from ₹25 lakh to ₹2 crore.

lesson.heading: Worked example and common mistakes
lesson.body:
Zenith Ltd, a public company that is not eligible under section 76, has paid-up capital ₹15 crore, free reserves ₹9 crore, securities premium ₹6 crore and revaluation reserve ₹5 crore. Member deposits outstanding are ₹4 crore.

| Particulars | ₹ crore |
| --- | --- |
| Paid-up share capital | 15.00 |
| Free reserves | 9.00 |
| Securities premium | 6.00 |
| **Base** (revaluation reserve excluded) | **30.00** |
| Limit: 35% | 10.50 |
| Less: outstanding | (4.00) |
| **Further deposits possible** | **6.50** |

Common mistakes:

- Including revaluation reserve in the base.
- Treating money from a relative of a director of a public company as exempt; that exemption is only for private companies.
- Forgetting that an advance for goods becomes a deposit once 365 days pass without appropriation.
- Confusing the deposit repayment reserve (20% of deposits maturing next year) with the debenture redemption reserve.

keyPoints: Deposit (2(31)) excludes receipts listed in rule 2(1)(c): government, banks, other companies, director with declaration, share application money allotted in 60 days.
Section 73(2): ordinary resolution, circular filed 30 days before issue, 20% deposit repayment reserve by 30 April.
Limits on paid-up capital + free reserves + securities premium: public (members) 35%, private (members) 100%, eligible company 10% members / 25% public.
Eligible company (76): net worth ₹100 crore or turnover ₹500 crore, special resolution, annual credit rating.
Tenure 6 to 36 months; short-term 3 months up to 10%.
DPT-3 by 30 June; section 76A fine on the company: at least ₹1 crore or twice the deposit (lower), up to ₹10 crore.

cases.title: Case: Bharat Cables Limited
cases.body:
Bharat Cables Limited is a public company. It is not an eligible company under section 76. Extract from its audited balance sheet at 31 March 2026:

| Particulars | ₹ crore |
| --- | --- |
| Paid-up equity share capital | 20.00 |
| General reserve (free) | 12.00 |
| Securities premium | 4.00 |
| Revaluation reserve | 3.00 |
| Deposits from members outstanding | 5.00 |
| Of which maturing in FY 2027-28 | 3.00 |

Receipts during FY 2026-27:

- ₹1.5 crore from Mr Desai, a director, with a written declaration that it is not out of borrowed funds.
- ₹80 lakh advance from a customer for supply of cables; the goods were not supplied and the advance was not adjusted for 400 days.
- ₹2 crore share application money received in July 2026; shares were neither allotted nor refunded for 90 days.
- ₹50 lakh loan from Unnati Finvest Private Limited, a company that is not an NBFC.

questions.prompt: Ignoring the FY 2026-27 receipts, what is the maximum amount of further deposits Bharat Cables can accept from its members under rule 3(3)? Answer in ₹ crore to 2 decimals.
questions.explanation:
Rule 3(3): a company under section 73(2) cannot accept member deposits that, with outstanding deposits, exceed 35% of paid-up share capital, free reserves and securities premium. Revaluation reserve is not a free reserve.

| Particulars | ₹ crore |
| --- | --- |
| Paid-up capital | 20.00 |
| Free reserves | 12.00 |
| Securities premium | 4.00 |
| **Base** | **36.00** |
| 35% of base | 12.60 |
| Less: outstanding deposits | (5.00) |
| **Further deposits possible** | **7.60** |

questions.prompt: Which of the FY 2026-27 receipts are treated as deposits? Select all that apply.
options: ₹80 lakh customer advance not adjusted for 400 days
₹2 crore share application money neither allotted nor refunded for 90 days
₹1.5 crore from Mr Desai with a declaration
₹50 lakh loan from Unnati Finvest Private Limited
questions.explanation: An advance for goods is excluded only if appropriated within 365 days; at 400 days it becomes a deposit. Share application money becomes a deposit if not allotted within 60 days and not refunded within the next 15 days. Money from a director with the required declaration and any amount received from another company are excluded under rule 2(1)(c).

questions.prompt: How much must Bharat Cables deposit in the deposit repayment reserve account by 30 April 2027, based on deposits maturing in FY 2027-28?
options: ₹60 lakh
₹1 crore
₹30 lakh
₹1.5 crore
questions.explanation: Section 73(2)(c) requires at least 20% of the deposits maturing during the following financial year: 20% of ₹3 crore = ₹60 lakh, kept in a separate scheduled bank account.

questions.prompt: If Mr Desai's son had lent ₹1 crore to Bharat Cables with a declaration that it was his own money, the amount would be:
options: A deposit, because the relative exemption applies only to private companies
Not a deposit, because relatives of directors are always exempt
Not a deposit, if the Board approves it
A deposit only if it carries interest
questions.explanation: Rule 2(1)(c)(viii) exempts money from a director of any company, and from a relative of a director only in the case of a private company, with the declaration. Bharat Cables is a public company, so its director's relative's money is a deposit.

questions.prompt: A public company can accept deposits from the public under section 76 if its net worth is at least ____ or turnover is at least ____.
options: ₹100 crore; ₹500 crore
₹50 crore; ₹250 crore
₹500 crore; ₹1,000 crore
₹10 crore; ₹100 crore
questions.explanation: Rule 2(1)(e) defines an eligible company as a public company with net worth of not less than ₹100 crore or turnover of not less than ₹500 crore, which has passed a special resolution and filed it with the Registrar.

questions.prompt: What are the minimum and maximum tenures for deposits under rule 3 (other than short-term deposits)?
options: 6 months and 36 months
3 months and 24 months
12 months and 60 months
6 months and 60 months
questions.explanation: Rule 3(1): deposits cannot be repayable earlier than 6 months or later than 36 months from acceptance or renewal. Short-term deposits for at least 3 months are allowed up to 10% of paid-up capital, free reserves and securities premium.

questions.prompt: The return of deposits in Form DPT-3 must be filed every year by:
options: 30 June, with information as on 31 March
30 September, with information as on 30 June
31 October, with information as on 31 March
30 April, with information as on 31 March
questions.explanation: Rule 16: every company to which the rules apply files a return of deposits on or before 30 June each year, containing information as on 31 March of that year, duly audited by the auditor.

questions.prompt: A banking company accepting deposits from the public must comply with Chapter V of the Companies Act, 2013.
questions.explanation: Section 73(1) excludes banking companies, NBFCs registered with RBI, housing finance companies registered with the National Housing Bank and other notified companies from Chapter V. They follow their own regulators.

questions.prompt: A private company that is a start-up may accept deposits from its members without the section 73(2)(a) to (e) conditions for 10 years from incorporation.
questions.explanation: Under the MCA exemption notification for private companies, a start-up is exempt from clauses (a) to (e) of section 73(2) for 10 years from incorporation, though it must file the details of monies accepted with the Registrar.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: under section 73(2)(c), at least ___ per cent of deposits maturing in the next financial year must be kept in the deposit repayment reserve account.
questions.explanation: The company must deposit at least 20% of the amount of deposits maturing during the following financial year in a scheduled bank account called the deposit repayment reserve account.

questions.prompt: List the receipts that are not deposits under rule 2(1)(c) of the Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules, 2014 (any eight).
questions.answer:
- Amounts received from the Central or State Government or guaranteed by it, or from a statutory authority.
- Amounts from foreign governments, foreign banks and multilateral institutions.
- Loans from banking companies, public financial institutions, insurance companies and scheduled banks.
- Amounts received from any other company.
- Subscription to securities, including share application money, if allotted within 60 days (or refunded within the next 15 days).
- Amounts from a director, or from a relative of a director of a private company, with a declaration that they are not borrowed.
- Secured bonds or debentures, and compulsorily convertible debentures, within the conditions.
- Non-interest-bearing security deposits from employees up to their annual salary.
- Advances for supply of goods or services appropriated within 365 days, and security or performance deposits.
- Unsecured loans from promoters under a stipulation of lending institutions.
- A start-up's convertible note of ₹25 lakh or more in a single tranche, convertible or repayable within 10 years.

questions.prompt: Decide with reasons: Shree Packaging Private Limited (paid-up capital ₹2 crore, free reserves ₹1 crore, securities premium nil) wants to accept ₹2.5 crore from its members without issuing a circular or creating a deposit repayment reserve. Advise.
questions.answer:
Provision: section 73(2) and rule 3, read with the MCA exemption notification for private companies.

Analysis: a private company is exempt from section 73(2)(a) to (e) (circular, filing with the Registrar 30 days before, deposit repayment reserve, certificate of no default, security) if it accepts from members an amount not exceeding 100% of the aggregate of its paid-up share capital, free reserves and securities premium. Base = ₹2 crore + ₹1 crore + nil = ₹3 crore. ₹2.5 crore is within 100% of ₹3 crore.

Conclusion: Shree Packaging can accept ₹2.5 crore from members without the circular and the deposit repayment reserve. It must still pass the resolution as required, file the details of monies accepted with the Registrar (DPT-3) and comply with the tenure, interest and register requirements of the rules.

questions.prompt: State the conditions under section 73(2) for a company to accept deposits from its members.
questions.answer:
- Ordinary resolution in general meeting, subject to the rules framed in consultation with RBI.
- Issue of a circular to members showing the financial position, credit rating, total deposits accepted, and particulars of any defaults.
- Filing a copy of the circular with the Registrar at least 30 days before the circular is issued.
- Depositing at least 20% of deposits maturing in the next financial year in a separate scheduled bank account (deposit repayment reserve account), on or before 30 April.
- Certifying that there has been no default in repayment of deposits or interest, or that any default was made good at least five years earlier.
- Providing security, where deposits are secured, by creating a charge on assets.
- Observing the limits (35% for public companies, 100% for private companies, of paid-up capital, free reserves and securities premium), the 6 to 36 month tenure and the interest ceiling.

questions.prompt: Explain the consequences under sections 75 and 76A of the Companies Act, 2013 for a company that accepts or fails to repay deposits in contravention of Chapter V.
questions.answer:
Section 75: if a company fails to repay a deposit or interest within the time specified, and it is proved that the deposit was accepted with intent to defraud depositors or for any fraudulent purpose, every officer responsible is personally liable, without any limitation of liability, for all or any losses or damages incurred by the depositors. Depositors may take legal action individually or as a class action under section 245.

Section 76A: where a company accepts, invites or renews deposits in contravention of Chapter V, or fails to repay within the time specified:
- the company must repay the deposit with interest and is punishable with a fine of not less than ₹1 crore or twice the amount of deposit accepted, whichever is lower, which may extend to ₹10 crore;
- every officer in default is punishable with imprisonment up to 7 years and a fine from ₹25 lakh to ₹2 crore.
- If the officer knowingly contravenes with intent to deceive, he is also liable for fraud under section 447.
