chapters.title: Registration of Charges
chapters.summary: What a charge is, the time limits and fees for registering it, the effect of non-registration, satisfaction of charges and the registers kept by the company and the Registrar.
chapters.lawAsOf: Companies Act 2013 sections 77-87 (as amended by the Companies (Amendment) Act 2019) and Companies (Registration of Charges) Rules 2014 as amended up to November 2026. Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill 2026 not yet enacted.

lesson.heading: Meaning of charge and duty to register
lesson.body:
Section 2(16): a charge is an interest or lien created on the property or assets of a company or any of its undertakings or both, as security, and includes a mortgage.

Section 77(1): every company creating a charge, within or outside India, on its property or assets or undertakings, whether tangible or otherwise, and situated in or outside India, must register the particulars with the Registrar. The particulars are signed by the company and the charge-holder and filed in Form CHG-1 (Form CHG-9 for debentures).

Time limits after the Companies (Amendment) Act 2019:

| Stage | Period (counted from creation of the charge) | Fees |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Normal | Within 30 days | Normal fees |
| First extension | Within 60 days of creation (on application to the Registrar) | Additional fees |
| Second extension | Within a further 60 days | Ad valorem fees |
| Beyond that | Only through the Central Government under section 87 | As ordered |

The same time limits apply to registration of a modification of the terms of a charge (section 79). On registration the Registrar issues a certificate of registration (CHG-2), which is conclusive evidence that the requirements of the Chapter were complied with.

lesson.heading: Effect of non-registration and registration by the charge-holder
lesson.body:
- **Section 77(3)**: a charge created by a company is not taken into account by the liquidator or any other creditor unless it is duly registered and a certificate of registration is issued.
- **Section 77(4)**: non-registration does not affect the contract or obligation for repayment of the money secured. The lender stays a creditor; it only loses its priority as a secured creditor.
- **Section 78**: if the company fails to register within 30 days, the charge-holder may apply to the Registrar. The Registrar gives the company notice; unless the company registers the charge or shows sufficient cause within 14 days, the Registrar allows the registration. The charge-holder can recover the fees from the company.
- **Section 80**: a person acquiring any property on which a charge is registered is deemed to have notice of the charge from the date of registration.
- **Section 87**: the Central Government may extend the time for registration or order rectification of an omission or misstatement if it is satisfied that the default was accidental or due to inadvertence or other sufficient cause, or is not of a nature to prejudice creditors or shareholders.

lesson.heading: Satisfaction, receivers and registers
lesson.body:
| Section | Event | Requirement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 82 | Payment or satisfaction of a charge | Company gives intimation to the Registrar in Form CHG-4 within 30 days. The Registrar sends notice to the charge-holder to show cause within 14 days; if no cause is shown, he records satisfaction. If the charge-holder gives the intimation, no notice is needed |
| 83 | Satisfaction recorded without intimation | Registrar may record satisfaction on evidence that the debt has been paid or the property released, even without the company's intimation |
| 84 | Appointment of receiver or manager | The person obtaining the order or making the appointment gives notice to the company and the Registrar within 30 days; the Registrar registers it (CHG-6) |
| 81 | Register of charges kept by the Registrar | Open to inspection by any person on payment of fees |
| 85 | Register of charges kept by the company | Kept at the registered office in Form CHG-7 with copies of instruments; open to inspection by members and creditors free of cost, and by others on payment of fees |

**Section 86 (penalty)**: if a company defaults on any provision of the Chapter, the company is liable to a penalty of ₹5 lakh and every officer in default to ₹50,000. Wilfully furnishing false or incorrect information or suppressing material information is fraud under section 447.

lesson.heading: Worked example and common mistakes
lesson.body:
A company creates a hypothecation charge on its stock in favour of a bank on 1 March.

| Filing date | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Day 25 after creation | Normal fees |
| Day 45 after creation | Allowed by the Registrar with additional fees (within 60 days) |
| Day 100 after creation | Allowed by the Registrar with ad valorem fees (within the further 60 days) |
| Day 140 after creation | Registrar cannot condone; apply to the Central Government under section 87 |

Common mistakes:

- Saying the loan becomes void if the charge is not registered; only the security is ineffective against the liquidator and other creditors.
- Forgetting that a charge on property outside India also needs registration.
- Mixing up the 30-day satisfaction intimation (section 82) with the 14-day show-cause period.

keyPoints: Charge (2(16)) = interest or lien on property as security, includes mortgage.
Register in CHG-1 within 30 days of creation; within 60 days with additional fees; a further 60 days with ad valorem fees (section 77).
Unregistered charge is not considered by the liquidator or other creditors, but the debt remains payable (77(3), 77(4)).
Charge-holder can register if company defaults; company gets 14 days' notice (section 78).
Satisfaction: CHG-4 within 30 days; charge-holder gets 14 days to show cause (section 82).
Section 87: Central Government may extend time or rectify; section 86 penalty ₹5 lakh company, ₹50,000 officer.

cases.title: Case: Kaveri Polymers Limited
cases.body:
Kaveri Polymers Limited took a term loan of ₹10 crore from Coastal Bank on 5 January 2026, secured by a mortgage on its factory in Hosur and by hypothecation of machinery imported and installed at its plant in Dubai.

- The company secretary resigned in January and no charge was filed by the company for the first 30 days.
- Coastal Bank wrote to the Registrar asking to register the charge itself.
- In a parallel draft plan, the CFO argues that if the charge is never registered "the bank's loan is void anyway, so we need not repay it".
- The company expects to repay the loan in full on 10 August 2026.

questions.prompt: If Kaveri itself files CHG-1 on the 50th day after creation of the charge, the Registrar may allow registration:
options: On payment of additional fees, as it is within 60 days of creation
Only on payment of ad valorem fees
Only with the approval of the Central Government
At normal fees, because the delay was due to the resignation of the company secretary
questions.explanation: The first proviso to section 77(1) lets the Registrar allow registration within 60 days of creation on payment of additional fees. Ad valorem fees apply only in the further 60-day period; the Central Government is needed only beyond that.

questions.prompt: Coastal Bank applies to the Registrar to register the charge under section 78. What must the Registrar do?
options: Give notice to Kaveri and allow registration unless the company registers it or shows sufficient cause within 14 days
Register the charge immediately without notice to the company
Reject the application, as only the company can register a charge
Refer the matter to the Tribunal
questions.explanation: Section 78: the charge-holder may apply where the company fails to register within 30 days. The Registrar gives the company notice and, unless it registers the charge or shows sufficient cause within 14 days, allows registration. The bank can recover the fees paid from the company.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the CFO's view that an unregistered charge makes the loan void.
options: Wrong: the charge is not taken into account by the liquidator and other creditors, but the debt remains payable
Right: an unregistered charge and the debt both become void
Right for the Dubai machinery only, since foreign assets are outside the Act
Wrong: an unregistered charge is fully valid against everyone
questions.explanation: Section 77(3) makes an unregistered charge ineffective against the liquidator and other creditors. Section 77(4) states that the contract or obligation for repayment is not affected. The bank becomes an unsecured creditor; the loan remains repayable.

questions.prompt: After repaying the loan on 10 August 2026, what must Kaveri do?
options: Intimate the Registrar of satisfaction in Form CHG-4 within 30 days
File CHG-1 again within 60 days
Nothing; the bank will close the charge
Intimate the Registrar within 7 days in Form CHG-7
questions.explanation: Section 82(1) requires the company to give intimation of payment or satisfaction in full of a registered charge to the Registrar within 30 days, in Form CHG-4. The Registrar then gives the charge-holder 14 days to show cause before recording satisfaction.

questions.prompt: Under section 85, the register of charges kept by the company is open to inspection by members and creditors:
options: Free of cost
On payment of a prescribed fee
Only with Board approval
Only during the AGM
questions.explanation: Section 85(2): the register of charges and the instruments of charge are open to inspection by members and creditors without fees, and by any other person on payment of the prescribed fee.

questions.prompt: A person buys land on which a registered charge exists. From when is the buyer deemed to have notice of the charge?
options: From the date of registration of the charge
From the date of the sale deed
Only if the seller tells him in writing
From the date the charge was created, even if never registered
questions.explanation: Section 80: where a charge is registered under section 77, any person acquiring the property is deemed to have notice of it from the date of registration.

questions.prompt: A company files particulars of a charge 140 days after creation. Who can allow registration?
options: The Central Government under section 87
The Registrar, with ad valorem fees
The Board of directors of the company
The charge-holder under section 78
questions.explanation: The Registrar can condone delay only up to 60 days of creation (additional fees) and a further 60 days (ad valorem fees). Beyond this, the company must apply to the Central Government under section 87 for extension of time.

questions.prompt: A charge created by an Indian company on its machinery located outside India does not require registration with the Registrar.
questions.explanation: Section 77(1) covers charges created within or outside India on property situated in or outside India.

questions.prompt: The certificate of registration of a charge issued by the Registrar is conclusive evidence that the requirements of Chapter VI as to registration were complied with.
questions.explanation: Section 77(2) makes the certificate conclusive evidence of compliance with the registration requirements.

questions.prompt: Which of these are consequences of a company's failure to register a charge? Select all that apply.
options: The liquidator will not take the charge into account
Other creditors are not bound by the charge
The company and officers in default are liable to penalty under section 86
The debt secured by the charge becomes void
The lender loses the right to sue the company for repayment
questions.explanation: Under section 77(3) the charge is not taken into account by the liquidator or other creditors, and section 86 imposes penalties. Section 77(4) preserves the debt, so the lender can still sue as an unsecured creditor.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: particulars of a charge (other than for debentures) are filed with the Registrar in Form ___.
questions.explanation: Form CHG-1 is used for creation or modification of charges; CHG-9 for debentures; CHG-4 for satisfaction.

questions.prompt: Explain the time limits for registration of a charge under section 77 and the effect of non-registration.
questions.answer:
Time limits (as amended in 2019):
- Particulars signed by the company and the charge-holder are filed within 30 days of creation.
- The Registrar may allow registration within 60 days of creation on payment of additional fees.
- If still not filed, the Registrar may allow it within a further 60 days on payment of ad valorem fees.
- The same limits apply to modification of a charge (section 79). Beyond them, the Central Government can extend time under section 87.

Effect of non-registration:
- Section 77(3): the charge is not taken into account by the liquidator or any other creditor; the lender loses priority as a secured creditor.
- Section 77(4): the obligation to repay the money secured is not affected.
- Section 86: penalty of ₹5 lakh on the company and ₹50,000 on every officer in default.
- The charge-holder may itself apply for registration under section 78.

questions.prompt: Decide with reasons: Bluefin Logistics Ltd created a charge on its vehicles in favour of Pioneer Finance on 1 April 2026 but did not register it. Bluefin went into liquidation in October 2026. Pioneer Finance claims priority over unsecured creditors. Decide.
questions.answer:
Provision: section 77(3) and (4) of the Companies Act, 2013.

Analysis: a charge is not taken into account by the liquidator or any other creditor unless it is duly registered under section 77(1) and a certificate is issued. Bluefin did not register the charge within 30 days, and neither the company nor Pioneer Finance (which could have applied under section 78) obtained registration within the extended periods. No order of the Central Government under section 87 exists.

Conclusion: Pioneer Finance cannot claim priority as a secured creditor in the liquidation. Under section 77(4) its debt is still payable, so it ranks as an unsecured creditor along with others. Bluefin and its officers in default are also liable to penalty under section 86.

questions.prompt: Describe the procedure for recording satisfaction of a charge under sections 82 and 83.
questions.answer:
Section 82:
- The company gives intimation of payment or satisfaction in full of a registered charge to the Registrar in Form CHG-4 within 30 days.
- The Registrar sends a notice to the charge-holder calling on it to show cause within 14 days why satisfaction should not be recorded.
- If no cause is shown, the Registrar records satisfaction in the register of charges and informs the company. If cause is shown, he records a note and informs the company.
- No notice is needed if the intimation is in the form signed by the charge-holder.

Section 83:
- The Registrar may, on evidence to his satisfaction, record that the debt has been paid or the property released or ceased to form part of the company's property, even without intimation from the company.
- He informs the parties within 30 days of recording.

questions.prompt: Explain the power of the Central Government under section 87 to rectify the register of charges.
questions.answer:
Under section 87 the Central Government (exercised by the Regional Director) may act where:
- the omission to give intimation of the creation, modification or satisfaction of a charge within the time required, or
- the omission or misstatement of any particular in the intimation,
was accidental or due to inadvertence or some other sufficient cause, or is not of a nature to prejudice the position of creditors or shareholders, or it is just and equitable to grant relief.

On the application of the company or any person interested, and on such terms as it thinks just, it may direct that the time for giving intimation be extended or that the omission or misstatement be rectified. An order extending time does not prejudice rights acquired in respect of the property before the charge is actually registered.

chapters.title: Management and Administration: Meetings, Resolutions and Annual Return
chapters.summary: Registers and annual return, the annual general meeting, extraordinary general meetings, notice, quorum, proxies, voting and resolutions under sections 88-122.
chapters.lawAsOf: Companies Act 2013 sections 88-122 and Companies (Management and Administration) Rules 2014 as amended up to November 2026. Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill 2026 not yet enacted.

lesson.heading: Registers and annual return
lesson.body:
- **Section 88**: every company keeps a register of members, a register of debenture-holders and a register of other security holders. An index is required where members exceed 50.
- **Section 94**: registers and returns are kept at the registered office. They may be kept at another place in India where more than one-tenth of the members reside, if approved by special resolution and notified to the Registrar.

Annual return (section 92):

| Point | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| Form | MGT-7 (MGT-7A for OPCs and small companies) |
| Content | Registered office, business activities, holding/subsidiary/associate companies, shares, debentures, indebtedness, members and changes, promoters, directors, KMP, meetings, remuneration, penalties |
| Signed by | A director and the company secretary; if there is no company secretary, a company secretary in practice. OPC and small company: the company secretary, or a director where there is none |
| Certification | Listed companies and companies with paid-up capital of ₹10 crore or more or turnover of ₹50 crore or more: certified by a company secretary in practice in Form MGT-8 |
| Due date | Filed with the Registrar within 60 days of the AGM (or of the last date on which it should have been held) |
| Website | If the company has a website, the annual return is placed there and the web link is given in the Board's report |

lesson.heading: Annual general meeting and extraordinary general meeting
lesson.body:
Section 96 (AGM): every company other than an OPC holds an AGM each year.

| Rule | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| First AGM | Within 9 months from the close of the first financial year; it need not be held in the year of incorporation |
| Later AGMs | Within 6 months from the close of the financial year, and not more than 15 months between two AGMs, whichever is earlier |
| Extension | Registrar may extend by up to 3 months for special reasons, but not for the first AGM |
| Time and place | During business hours (9 a.m. to 6 p.m.), on a day that is not a national holiday, at the registered office or another place in the same city, town or village |

Ordinary business at an AGM (section 102(2)): consideration of financial statements and reports of the Board and auditors; declaration of dividend; appointment of directors in place of those retiring; appointment of auditors and fixing their remuneration. All other business is special business and needs an explanatory statement disclosing material facts and the interest of directors, KMP and their relatives.

Section 100 (EGM): the Board may call an EGM at any time. Members holding at least one-tenth of the paid-up capital carrying voting rights (or one-tenth of voting power in a company without share capital) may requisition one. If the Board does not, within 21 days of the requisition, proceed to call a meeting to be held within 45 days, the requisitionists may themselves call and hold it within 3 months of the requisition. The company reimburses their reasonable expenses and recovers them from the defaulting directors' fees.

lesson.heading: Notice, quorum, proxies and voting
lesson.body:
- **Notice (section 101)**: at least 21 clear days in writing or electronic mode, to every member, legal representative of a deceased member, assignee of an insolvent member, auditors and directors. Shorter notice: for an AGM, consent of at least 95% of members entitled to vote; for any other meeting, a majority in number of members entitled to vote who hold at least 95% of the paid-up share capital carrying voting rights.
- **Quorum (section 103)**, unless the articles require more:

| Company | Members personally present |
| --- | --- |
| Private company | 2 |
| Public company, up to 1,000 members | 5 |
| Public company, 1,001 to 5,000 members | 15 |
| Public company, more than 5,000 members | 30 |

If the quorum is not present within half an hour, the meeting stands adjourned to the same day next week at the same time and place (or as the Board decides); a meeting called by requisitionists is cancelled. At the adjourned meeting, the members present form the quorum.

- **Proxies (section 105)**: a member entitled to vote may appoint a proxy, who need not be a member. A proxy cannot speak and can vote only on a poll. A person can be proxy for not more than 50 members holding in aggregate not more than 10% of the total voting share capital. The proxy form is deposited at least 48 hours before the meeting. A section 8 company's members cannot appoint proxies unless its articles allow.
- **Voting**: show of hands (section 107), electronic voting (section 108, for listed companies and companies with 1,000 or more members), poll (section 109) and postal ballot (section 110).

lesson.heading: Resolutions, filing and minutes
lesson.body:
| Resolution | Section | Requirement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ordinary | 114(1) | Votes cast in favour (including the chairman's casting vote, if any) exceed votes cast against |
| Special | 114(2) | Intention to propose as special resolution stated in the notice; notice duly given; votes cast in favour at least three times the votes cast against |
| Special notice | 115 | Required where the Act or articles say so (removal of a director under section 169, appointing an auditor other than the retiring one). Given by members holding at least 1% of total voting power or shares with at least ₹5 lakh paid up, not earlier than 3 months but at least 14 days before the meeting |

Worked example: votes in favour 6,40,000; against 2,10,000; abstained 90,000. 3 x 2,10,000 = 6,30,000. 6,40,000 is more than 6,30,000, so the special resolution passes. Abstentions are ignored.

- **Section 117**: copies of special resolutions and specified agreements and resolutions are filed with the Registrar in Form MGT-14 within 30 days.
- **Section 118**: minutes of every general meeting, Board meeting and committee meeting are prepared, signed and kept within 30 days. Minutes kept in accordance with the section are evidence of the proceedings.
- **Section 122**: AGM provisions do not apply to an OPC; a resolution communicated by its member and entered in the minute book is deemed passed at a meeting.

**Common mistakes**: counting abstentions in a special resolution; letting proxies speak; forgetting that the 15-month gap and the 6-month limit apply together.

keyPoints: AGM: first within 9 months of end of first FY; later within 6 months of FY end and 15 months of last AGM; ROC extension up to 3 months (not first AGM).
Notice 21 clear days; shorter notice: AGM 95% of members; other meetings majority in number holding 95% of voting capital.
Quorum: private 2; public 5 / 15 / 30 for up to 1,000 / up to 5,000 / above 5,000 members.
Proxy: cannot speak, votes only on poll, max 50 members and 10% of voting capital, form 48 hours before.
Special resolution: votes in favour at least 3 times votes against (114(2)); special notice 1% or ₹5 lakh, 14 days (115).
EGM requisition: one-tenth of paid-up voting capital; Board acts within 21 days, meeting within 45 days; else requisitionists within 3 months.
Annual return MGT-7 within 60 days of AGM; MGT-8 certification if listed, paid-up ₹10 crore or turnover ₹50 crore.

cases.title: Case: Lotus Hospitality Limited
cases.body:
Lotus Hospitality Limited is an unlisted public company with 3,400 members, paid-up capital of ₹30 crore and turnover of ₹180 crore. Its financial year ends on 31 March. The last AGM was held on 20 September 2025. The articles have no special quorum provision.

At the AGM for FY 2025-26:

- Mr Rao, a member, has appointed his friend Mr Jain (not a member) as proxy. Mr Jain wants to speak on the dividend proposal.
- A special resolution to alter the articles received 7,20,000 votes in favour, 2,50,000 votes against and 1,00,000 abstentions.
- The company has no company secretary in employment.

questions.prompt: By what date must Lotus hold its AGM for FY 2025-26 (without any extension)?
options: 30 September 2026
20 December 2026
31 December 2026
20 September 2026
questions.explanation: Section 96(1): within 6 months from the close of the financial year (30 September 2026) or 15 months from the previous AGM (20 December 2026), whichever is earlier. So 30 September 2026.

questions.prompt: What is the quorum for Lotus's general meeting?
options: 15 members personally present
5 members personally present
30 members personally present
2 members personally present
questions.explanation: Section 103(1)(a)(ii): for a public company with more than 1,000 but up to 5,000 members, the quorum is 15 members personally present, unless the articles require more.

questions.prompt: Can Mr Jain, as proxy for Mr Rao, speak on the dividend proposal?
options: No, a proxy has no right to speak and can vote only on a poll
Yes, a proxy has all the rights of the member
Yes, but only if he is also a member
No, because a non-member cannot be appointed proxy
questions.explanation: Section 105(1): a proxy need not be a member, but has no right to speak at the meeting and is not entitled to vote except on a poll.

questions.prompt: Is the special resolution to alter the articles passed?
options: No, votes in favour (7,20,000) are less than three times votes against (7,50,000)
Yes, because votes in favour exceed votes against
Yes, because abstentions are added to votes in favour
No, because abstentions exceed 10% of votes
questions.explanation: Section 114(2)(c): votes cast in favour must be at least three times the votes cast against. 3 x 2,50,000 = 7,50,000, and 7,20,000 is less. Abstentions are not votes cast and are ignored.

questions.prompt: Who signs and certifies Lotus's annual return?
options: Signed by a director and a company secretary in practice, and certified by a company secretary in practice in Form MGT-8
Signed by any one director only; no certification needed
Signed by the statutory auditor
Signed by two directors; certified by the Registrar
questions.explanation: Section 92(1): where there is no company secretary, the annual return is signed by a director and a company secretary in practice. Section 92(2) with rule 11(2): companies with paid-up capital of ₹10 crore or more or turnover of ₹50 crore or more need certification by a practising CS in MGT-8. Lotus meets both tests.

questions.prompt: Members of a company can requisition an extraordinary general meeting if they hold at least:
options: One-tenth of the paid-up share capital carrying voting rights
One-fourth of the paid-up share capital
5% of the paid-up share capital
51% of the voting power
questions.explanation: Section 100(2)(a): members holding, on the date of requisition, at least one-tenth of the paid-up share capital that carries voting rights may requisition an EGM.

questions.prompt: An AGM can be called at shorter notice than 21 clear days if consent is given by:
options: At least 95% of the members entitled to vote
A majority of members holding 75% of paid-up capital
All the directors
Members holding 51% of voting power
questions.explanation: Proviso to section 101(1): for an AGM, consent in writing or electronically of not less than 95% of the members entitled to vote. For other meetings, a majority in number holding at least 95% of the paid-up voting share capital.

questions.prompt: A special notice under section 115 must be given to the company:
options: Not earlier than 3 months but at least 14 days before the meeting
At least 21 days before the meeting
At least 7 days before the meeting
Within 30 days after the meeting
questions.explanation: Rule 23: special notice is given by members holding at least 1% of total voting power or shares with at least ₹5 lakh paid up, not earlier than 3 months but at least 14 days before the meeting. The company informs members at least 7 days before the meeting.

questions.prompt: A proxy can vote on a show of hands at a general meeting.
questions.explanation: Section 105(1) proviso: a proxy is not entitled to vote except on a poll.

questions.prompt: A One Person Company is not required to hold an annual general meeting.
questions.explanation: Section 96(1) excludes an OPC. Under section 122, a resolution communicated by the member and entered in the minute book is deemed passed at a meeting.

questions.prompt: Which of these items are ordinary business at an AGM under section 102(2)? Select all that apply.
options: Consideration of financial statements and reports of the Board and auditors
Declaration of dividend
Appointment of directors in place of those retiring
Appointment of auditors and fixing their remuneration
Alteration of articles of association
Issue of bonus shares
questions.explanation: These four items are ordinary business. Everything else, including alteration of articles and bonus issue, is special business needing an explanatory statement.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: special resolutions must be filed with the Registrar in Form MGT-14 within ___ days of passing.
questions.explanation: Section 117(1): resolutions and agreements covered by section 117(3) are filed within 30 days of passing or making them.

questions.prompt: Explain the procedure for calling an extraordinary general meeting on the requisition of members under section 100.
questions.answer:
- The Board may call an EGM whenever it thinks fit (section 100(1)).
- Requisition: members holding at least one-tenth of the paid-up share capital carrying voting rights (or one-tenth of total voting power in a company without share capital) may deliver a signed requisition at the registered office, stating the matters to be considered.
- If the Board does not, within 21 days of receipt of a valid requisition, proceed to call a meeting to be held within 45 days, the requisitionists may call and hold the meeting themselves within 3 months of the requisition.
- The meeting is called in the same manner as a Board-called meeting, with 21 clear days' notice and explanatory statement.
- The company reimburses the requisitionists' reasonable expenses and recovers them from the fees or remuneration of the directors in default.
- If quorum is not present within half an hour, a requisitioned meeting stands cancelled.

questions.prompt: Decide with reasons: Aster Ltd (a public company with 800 members) called its AGM on 26 January 2026 at 11 a.m. at a hotel in the same city as its registered office. A shareholder says the meeting is invalid. Decide.
questions.answer:
Provision: section 96(2). An AGM is called during business hours (9 a.m. to 6 p.m.) on a day that is not a national holiday, at the registered office or some other place within the city, town or village where the registered office is situated.

Analysis: the time (11 a.m.) and the place (a hotel in the same city) comply. However, 26 January is Republic Day, a national holiday. "National holiday" means a day declared as such by the Central Government.

Conclusion: the AGM was called on a national holiday, contrary to section 96(2). The shareholder's objection is valid and the meeting is not properly held. The company should hold the AGM on a valid day within the time limits of section 96(1).

questions.prompt: Decide with reasons: at the AGM of Coral Ltd (a public company with 2,600 members), only 11 members were present half an hour after the scheduled time. The chairman proceeded with the meeting and passed all resolutions. Are the resolutions valid?
questions.answer:
Provision: section 103. For a public company with more than 1,000 but up to 5,000 members, the quorum is 15 members personally present, unless the articles specify more. Under section 103(2), if the quorum is not present within half an hour, the meeting stands adjourned to the same day in the next week at the same time and place, or to such other date and place as the Board decides.

Analysis: only 11 members were present, below the quorum of 15. The chairman had no power to continue.

Conclusion: the resolutions passed are invalid. The meeting stood adjourned. At the adjourned meeting, if quorum is still not present within half an hour, the members present form the quorum and can transact the business.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between an ordinary resolution and a special resolution, and state when special notice is required.
questions.answer:
Ordinary resolution (section 114(1)): passed where the notice is duly given and the votes cast in favour (on show of hands, electronically or on poll, including the chairman's casting vote) exceed the votes cast against.

Special resolution (section 114(2)): the intention to propose it as a special resolution is specifically stated in the notice; notice is duly given; and votes cast in favour are at least three times the votes cast against.

Uses: ordinary resolution for ordinary business and matters the Act does not reserve; special resolution for matters such as alteration of articles or MOA, buy-back above 10%, preferential issue, and change of registered office outside the local limits.

Special notice (section 115): needed where the Act or articles require it, for example removal of a director (section 169) or appointment of an auditor other than the retiring auditor (section 140(4)). Members holding at least 1% of total voting power or shares with ₹5 lakh paid up give it at least 14 days (and not more than 3 months) before the meeting.

chapters.title: Declaration and Payment of Dividend
chapters.summary: Sources of dividend, declaration out of reserves, interim dividend, payment timelines, unpaid dividend, IEPF transfer and penalties under sections 123-127.
chapters.lawAsOf: Companies Act 2013 sections 123-127 and Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules 2014 as amended up to November 2026. Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill 2026 not yet enacted.

lesson.heading: Sources of dividend (section 123(1))
lesson.body:
A company can declare or pay dividend only out of:

- profits of the current financial year, after providing for depreciation under section 123(2) (Schedule II);
- profits of previous financial years, after depreciation, remaining undistributed; or both;
- money provided by the Central or State Government for payment of dividend under a guarantee.

Further rules:

- Before declaring dividend, the company must set off carried-over losses and depreciation not provided in previous years against the profits of the current year.
- In computing profits, unrealised gains, notional gains, revaluation of assets and changes in carrying amount of assets or liabilities on fair value measurement are excluded.
- Transfer to reserves before declaring dividend is optional; the company may transfer such percentage of profits as it considers appropriate.
- Dividend cannot be declared out of reserves other than free reserves.
- Section 123(6): a company that has failed to comply with sections 73 and 74 (deposits) cannot declare dividend on equity shares while the failure continues.
- Dividend is paid only in cash (cheque, warrant or electronic mode) to the registered holder or to his order or his banker. Capitalising profits or reserves for bonus shares is permitted.

lesson.heading: Declaration out of reserves when profits are inadequate (rule 3)
lesson.body:
If profits for the year are inadequate or absent, a company may declare dividend out of free reserves accumulated from earlier years, subject to all of these conditions:

| Condition | Limit |
| --- | --- |
| Rate | Not more than the average of the rates declared in the 3 immediately preceding years (not applicable if no dividend was declared in each of those 3 years) |
| Amount drawn | Not more than one-tenth of paid-up share capital plus free reserves as per the latest audited financial statements |
| Order of use | The amount drawn is first used to set off losses of the current year, before any equity dividend is declared |
| Balance left | Reserves remaining after the withdrawal must be at least 15% of paid-up share capital as per the latest audited financial statements |

Worked example: paid-up capital ₹20 crore, free reserves ₹14 crore, current year loss ₹1 crore, past rates 9%, 11% and 10%.

| Check | Working | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Maximum rate | (9 + 11 + 10) / 3 | 10% |
| Dividend at 10% | 10% x ₹20 crore | ₹2 crore |
| Amount to draw | Loss ₹1 crore + dividend ₹2 crore | ₹3 crore |
| Ceiling on drawing | 1/10 x (20 + 14) | ₹3.4 crore: within limit |
| Balance reserves | 14 - 3 = 11 vs 15% x 20 = 3 | Within limit |

lesson.heading: Interim dividend and payment timeline
lesson.body:
**Interim dividend (section 123(3))**: declared by the Board during the financial year, or at any time from the close of the year until the AGM, out of the surplus in the profit and loss account or the profits of the year for which it is declared or generated up to the quarter before declaration. If the company has incurred a loss in the current year up to the end of the quarter immediately preceding declaration, the interim dividend rate cannot exceed the average rate of the 3 preceding years.

Payment timeline:

| Step | Section | Time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Deposit dividend amount (including interim) in a separate scheduled bank account | 123(4) | Within 5 days of declaration |
| Pay dividend or post warrant | 127 | Within 30 days of declaration |
| Transfer unpaid amount to Unpaid Dividend Account in a scheduled bank | 124(1) | Within 7 days after the 30 days expire |
| Place statement of unpaid amounts and names on website | 124(2) | Within 90 days of the transfer |
| Interest if the unpaid amount is not transferred | 124(1) | 12% per annum from the date of default |
| Transfer to Investor Education and Protection Fund | 124(5) | Amounts unpaid or unclaimed for 7 years from transfer to the Unpaid Dividend Account |
| Transfer shares to IEPF | 124(6) | Shares on which dividend is unpaid or unclaimed for 7 consecutive years |

Claimants can claim their transferred dividend and shares from the IEPF under section 125.

lesson.heading: Punishment for failure to distribute (section 127)

keyPoints: Dividend only out of current or past profits after depreciation, or government money under guarantee (123(1)); unrealised and revaluation gains excluded.
From reserves: rate up to 3-year average; draw up to 1/10 of paid-up capital + free reserves; set off current loss first; leave reserves of at least 15% of paid-up capital.
Interim dividend by the Board; if loss up to the preceding quarter, rate capped at 3-year average.
Deposit in separate bank account within 5 days; pay within 30 days; Unpaid Dividend Account within 7 days after that.
IEPF: unpaid for 7 years, and shares with 7 consecutive years of unclaimed dividend (124(5), (6)).
Section 127: director imprisonment up to 2 years and fine of at least ₹1,000 a day; company pays 18% interest.

cases.title: Case: Sahyadri Steel Limited
cases.body:
Sahyadri Steel Limited wants to declare a final dividend for FY 2026-27 although it has incurred a loss of ₹3 crore for that year. Data from its latest audited financial statements:

| Particulars | ₹ crore |
| --- | --- |
| Paid-up equity share capital (₹10 shares) | 50.00 |
| Free reserves | 40.00 |
| Revaluation reserve | 12.00 |

| Year | Dividend rate |
| --- | --- |
| FY 2023-24 | 12% |
| FY 2024-25 | 10% |
| FY 2025-26 | 8% |

The Board proposes a 12% dividend, to be met from free reserves. The company has no default in repayment of deposits.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum amount Sahyadri can draw from its free reserves under rule 3 for this purpose? Answer in ₹ crore to 2 decimals.
questions.explanation:
Rule 3(3): the total amount drawn from accumulated profits cannot exceed one-tenth of the sum of paid-up share capital and free reserves as per the latest audited financial statements. Revaluation reserve is not a free reserve.

| Particulars | ₹ crore |
| --- | --- |
| Paid-up share capital | 50.00 |
| Free reserves | 40.00 |
| **Total** | **90.00** |
| One-tenth | **9.00** |

questions.prompt: What is the maximum rate of dividend Sahyadri can declare out of reserves?
questions.explanation: Rule 3(2): the rate cannot exceed the average of the rates declared in the three preceding years: (12 + 10 + 8) / 3 = 10%. The proposed 12% is not permitted.

questions.prompt: If Sahyadri declares the maximum permissible dividend, how much must it draw from free reserves in total?
options: ₹8 crore
₹5 crore
₹9 crore
₹6 crore
questions.explanation: Dividend at 10% on ₹50 crore = ₹5 crore. Under rule 3(4), the amount drawn is first used to set off the current year's loss of ₹3 crore. Total drawn = ₹3 crore + ₹5 crore = ₹8 crore, within the ₹9 crore ceiling. Balance reserves of ₹32 crore exceed 15% of paid-up capital (₹7.5 crore).

questions.prompt: The Board suggests using the revaluation reserve of ₹12 crore to pay a higher dividend. This is:
options: Not allowed, because dividend cannot be paid out of reserves created by revaluation of assets
Allowed, if approved by special resolution
Allowed up to 15% of paid-up capital
Allowed, because the reserve appears in audited accounts
questions.explanation: Section 123(1) excludes revaluation and notional or unrealised gains from profits available for dividend, and dividend from reserves can come only from free reserves. A revaluation reserve is not a free reserve.

questions.prompt: Within how many days of declaration must the amount of dividend be deposited in a separate bank account?
options: 5 days
7 days
30 days
15 days
questions.explanation: Section 123(4): the dividend amount, including interim dividend, is deposited in a scheduled bank in a separate account within 5 days from the date of declaration.

questions.prompt: Dividend declared on 10 September remains unpaid on 10 October. By when must the unpaid amount be transferred to the Unpaid Dividend Account?
options: Within 7 days after the 30-day period expires
Within 30 days after the 30-day period expires
Within 90 days of declaration
Within 7 years
questions.explanation: Section 124(1): within 7 days from the expiry of 30 days from declaration, the company transfers the unpaid or unclaimed dividend to the Unpaid Dividend Account in a scheduled bank.

questions.prompt: Money in the Unpaid Dividend Account that remains unpaid or unclaimed for ____ years from the date of transfer goes to the IEPF.
questions.explanation: Section 124(5): amounts unpaid or unclaimed for seven years from the date of transfer to the Unpaid Dividend Account are transferred to the IEPF. Shares with dividend unclaimed for seven consecutive years also move to the IEPF (124(6)).

questions.prompt: A company may pay dividend by distributing its products to shareholders, if the articles allow.
questions.explanation: Section 123(5): dividend is payable only in cash, which includes cheque, warrant and electronic mode. Capitalisation of profits for bonus shares is the only non-cash form allowed.

questions.prompt: A company that has defaulted in repaying deposits accepted under section 73 cannot declare dividend on its equity shares while the default continues.
questions.explanation: Section 123(6) bars a company that fails to comply with sections 73 and 74 from declaring any dividend on equity shares.

questions.prompt: In which situations is non-payment of dividend within 30 days NOT an offence under section 127? Select all that apply.
options: There is a dispute about the right to receive the dividend
The dividend was lawfully adjusted against a sum due from the shareholder
The dividend could not be paid by operation of law
The company had a temporary cash shortage
The directors were busy with a merger
questions.explanation: The proviso to section 127 lists operation of law, shareholder directions that could not be complied with, disputes about the right to receive, lawful adjustment against dues, and other reasons not due to the company's default. Cash shortage or management convenience is the company's own default.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: under section 127, a company that fails to pay dividend within 30 days pays simple interest at ___ per cent per annum during the default.
questions.explanation: Section 127: the company is liable to pay simple interest at 18% per annum for the period of default, in addition to the punishment of directors.

questions.prompt: State the conditions under which a company may declare dividend out of free reserves when profits for the year are inadequate (rule 3).
questions.answer:
Under the second proviso to section 123(1) read with rule 3 of the Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules, 2014:

- Rate: not more than the average of the rates declared in the three years immediately preceding. This does not apply if the company has not declared any dividend in each of those three years.
- Amount: the total drawn from accumulated profits cannot exceed one-tenth of the sum of paid-up share capital and free reserves as per the latest audited financial statements.
- Order: the amount drawn is first used to set off losses incurred in the financial year in which dividend is declared, before any dividend on equity shares.
- Balance: reserves remaining after the withdrawal must be at least 15% of paid-up share capital as per the latest audited financial statements.
- Only free reserves can be used; revaluation and other non-free reserves are excluded.

questions.prompt: Explain the provisions of section 123(3) relating to interim dividend.
questions.answer:
- The Board of directors may declare interim dividend during any financial year, or at any time during the period from the closure of the financial year until the AGM.
- Source: surplus in the profit and loss account, or profits of the financial year for which it is declared, or profits generated in the year up to the quarter preceding the date of declaration.
- Restriction: if the company has incurred a loss during the current year up to the end of the quarter immediately preceding the declaration, the interim dividend cannot exceed the average dividend rate declared in the three preceding financial years.
- The amount is deposited in a separate bank account within 5 days of declaration (section 123(4)) and paid within 30 days (section 127).
- Interim dividend does not need members' approval when declared, though it is usually confirmed at the AGM.

questions.prompt: Decide with reasons: Galaxy Ltd declared a dividend on 1 August 2026. Mr Saxena's dividend of ₹40,000 was not paid because Galaxy adjusted it against ₹55,000 that he owed the company as unpaid calls on partly paid shares. Mr Saxena alleges an offence under section 127. Decide.
questions.answer:
Provision: section 127 punishes directors and makes the company liable to 18% interest when declared dividend is not paid within 30 days. Clause (d) of the proviso says no offence is committed where the dividend has been lawfully adjusted by the company against any sum due to it from the shareholder.

Analysis: unpaid calls on partly paid shares are a sum due from Mr Saxena to Galaxy. Articles of companies generally permit deduction of such sums from dividends (Table F permits deduction of sums presently payable by the member on account of calls). The adjustment of ₹40,000 against ₹55,000 due is a lawful adjustment.

Conclusion: no offence under section 127 is committed, and no interest is payable. Mr Saxena still owes ₹15,000 on the calls.

questions.prompt: Decide with reasons: Delta Ltd's profit for the year includes ₹6 crore of unrealised gain on fair valuation of investments. Its profit after depreciation is ₹10 crore. The Board wants to declare dividend of ₹9 crore out of the current year's profit. Advise.
questions.answer:
Provision: section 123(1), as amended by the Companies (Amendment) Act 2015, states that in computing profits for declaring dividend, a company shall not include unrealised gains, notional gains, revaluation of assets or any change in carrying amount of an asset or liability on measurement at fair value.

Analysis: distributable current-year profit = ₹10 crore - ₹6 crore unrealised gain = ₹4 crore (assuming no carried-forward losses or unprovided depreciation to set off).

Conclusion: Delta can declare dividend of up to ₹4 crore out of the current year's profit. For the balance it would need undistributed profits of earlier years, or it must follow rule 3 if it uses free reserves. A dividend of ₹9 crore out of current profit is not permitted.

chapters.title: Accounts of Companies, and Audit and Auditors
chapters.summary: Books of account, financial statements, Board's report, CSR, filing, internal audit, and the appointment, rotation, eligibility, removal, duties and prohibited services of statutory auditors.
chapters.lawAsOf: Companies Act 2013 sections 128-148, Companies (Accounts) Rules 2014, Companies (CSR Policy) Rules 2014 and Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules 2014 as amended up to November 2026. Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill 2026 (proposes a higher CSR profit threshold) not yet enacted.

lesson.heading: Books of account and financial statements
lesson.body:
| Section | Provision |
| --- | --- |
| 128 | Books of account on accrual basis and double entry, kept at the registered office or another place in India decided by the Board (Registrar informed within 7 days). Electronic books must be accessible in India at all times, with a daily back-up on servers located in India. Preserved for at least 8 years. Directors may inspect. Responsibility: MD, whole-time director in charge of finance, CFO or other person charged by the Board |
| 129 | Financial statements give a true and fair view, comply with notified accounting standards and are in the form in Schedule III. A company with subsidiaries, associates or joint ventures also prepares consolidated financial statements and attaches Form AOC-1 |
| 130 | Re-opening of accounts only on an order of a court or the Tribunal (fraud, or mismanagement casting doubt on reliability), not beyond 8 financial years before the current year |
| 131 | Voluntary revision by the Board, with Tribunal approval, for any of the 3 preceding financial years, not more than once in a financial year |
| 134 | Financial statements approved by the Board and signed by the chairperson (if authorised) or two directors (one being MD), and by the CEO, CFO and company secretary where appointed. The Board's report covers the matters in section 134(3), including the directors' responsibility statement |
| 136 | Copies of financial statements sent to members at least 21 days before the AGM (shorter where the AGM is called on shorter notice) |
| 137 | Financial statements filed with the Registrar within 30 days of the AGM (AOC-4); if not adopted, unadopted statements within 30 days and adopted ones within 30 days of the adjourned meeting. An OPC files within 180 days from the close of the financial year |

lesson.heading: Corporate social responsibility (section 135) and internal audit (section 138)
lesson.body:
CSR applies to a company that, during the immediately preceding financial year, has:

- net worth of ₹500 crore or more, or
- turnover of ₹1,000 crore or more, or
- net profit of ₹5 crore or more.

| Point | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Spend | At least 2% of average net profits (computed under section 198) of the 3 immediately preceding financial years |
| CSR committee | Required, with at least 3 directors (one independent where applicable). Not required where the CSR obligation is up to ₹50 lakh; the Board then discharges its functions |
| Unspent, not ongoing project | Transfer to a fund in Schedule VII within 6 months of the end of the financial year |
| Unspent, ongoing project | Transfer to an Unspent CSR Account within 30 days of the end of the year, and spend within 3 financial years |
| Excess spent | Can be set off against the requirement of up to 3 succeeding financial years |

Worked example: net profits ₹12 crore, ₹15 crore and ₹18 crore. Average = ₹15 crore. CSR = 2% x ₹15 crore = ₹30 lakh. No CSR committee is needed as it is within ₹50 lakh.

Internal audit (section 138, rule 13) is compulsory for listed companies; unlisted public companies with paid-up capital of ₹50 crore or more, or turnover of ₹200 crore or more, or borrowings of ₹100 crore or more, or deposits of ₹25 crore or more; and private companies with turnover of ₹200 crore or more or borrowings of ₹100 crore or more. The internal auditor may be a CA, a CMA or another professional, and need not be an employee.

lesson.heading: Appointment and rotation of auditors (section 139)
lesson.body:
| Situation | Appointed by | Time limit and tenure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First auditor, non-government company | Board | Within 30 days of registration; if the Board fails, members at an EGM within 90 days. Holds office till the first AGM |
| First auditor, government company | CAG | Within 60 days of registration; if CAG fails, the Board within 30 days; if the Board fails, members at an EGM within 60 days |
| Subsequent auditor | Members at AGM | From the conclusion of that AGM to the conclusion of the sixth AGM (5 years) |
| Casual vacancy | Board | Within 30 days. If caused by resignation, the appointment is also approved by members at a general meeting within 3 months of the Board's recommendation; holds office till the next AGM |

Rotation (section 139(2), rule 5) applies to listed companies; unlisted public companies with paid-up capital of ₹10 crore or more; private companies with paid-up capital of ₹50 crore or more; and all other companies with public borrowings from financial institutions or banks, or public deposits, of ₹50 crore or more. OPCs and small companies are excluded.

- Individual auditor: not more than one term of 5 consecutive years.
- Audit firm: not more than two terms of 5 consecutive years.
- Cooling-off: 5 years, during which the individual or firm (or a firm with a common partner) cannot be reappointed.

lesson.heading: Eligibility, removal, resignation, duties and prohibited services
lesson.body:
Section 141(3): the following cannot be appointed as auditor.

- A body corporate (other than an LLP).
- An officer or employee of the company, or a partner or employee of such a person.
- A person who, or whose relative or partner, holds securities of the company, its subsidiary, holding or associate company. A relative may hold securities with face value up to ₹1 lakh.
- A person, relative or partner indebted to the company (or group) above ₹5 lakh, or who has given a guarantee or security for a third person's debt to it above ₹1 lakh.
- A person with a business relationship with the company or group.
- A person whose relative is a director or KMP of the company.
- A person in full-time employment elsewhere, or who is already auditor of 20 companies.
- A person convicted of fraud, for 10 years from conviction.
- A person rendering any service under section 144 to the company or its holding or subsidiary.

Section 140: removal before the term needs a special resolution and prior approval of the Central Government, with the auditor given a reasonable opportunity of being heard. A resigning auditor files Form ADT-3 with the company and the Registrar within 30 days. Appointing someone other than the retiring auditor at an AGM needs special notice.

Section 143: auditor's right of access to books and vouchers, duty to report on true and fair view and specified matters, and to report fraud. Fraud of ₹1 crore or more is reported to the Central Government; smaller fraud to the audit committee or Board.

Section 144 prohibited services (directly or indirectly): accounting and book-keeping, internal audit, design and implementation of financial information systems, actuarial services, investment advisory services, investment banking services, outsourced financial services and management services.

**Common mistakes**: applying rotation to a small company; counting the relative's ₹1 lakh limit as applying to the auditor himself; forgetting Central Government approval for removal.

keyPoints: Books at registered office, preserved 8 years; electronic back-up on Indian servers daily (128).
Revision of financial statements: voluntary with Tribunal approval for 3 preceding years (131); re-opening only on court or Tribunal order, up to 8 years (130).
CSR: net worth ₹500 crore or turnover ₹1,000 crore or net profit ₹5 crore; spend 2% of 3-year average; no committee if obligation up to ₹50 lakh.
Auditor: first by Board within 30 days; then members for 5 years (AGM to sixth AGM).
Rotation: individual 1 term, firm 2 terms of 5 years, cooling-off 5 years; listed, unlisted public ₹10 crore, private ₹50 crore paid-up, or ₹50 crore borrowings/deposits.
Disqualification: relative's holding above ₹1 lakh, debt above ₹5 lakh, guarantee above ₹1 lakh, more than 20 audits (141(3)).
Removal: special resolution + Central Government approval; resignation ADT-3 in 30 days (140).

cases.title: Case: Indus Pharma Limited
cases.body:
Indus Pharma Limited is an unlisted public company with paid-up capital of ₹60 crore, turnover of ₹420 crore and no deposits.

| Financial year | Net profit under section 198 (₹ crore) |
| --- | --- |
| 2023-24 | 18 |
| 2024-25 | 24 |
| 2025-26 | 30 |

Its statutory auditor, AB and Co. (a firm), was first appointed at the AGM of 2016 and re-appointed at the AGM of 2021 for a further 5 years. For the AGM of 2026 the Board is considering CD and Associates as auditor. The wife of a partner of CD and Associates holds Indus equity shares of face value ₹80,000. Indus has no internal auditor.

questions.prompt: What is the minimum CSR spend for Indus Pharma in FY 2026-27? Answer in ₹ lakh, rounded to the nearest lakh.
questions.explanation:
Section 135 applies because net profit for FY 2025-26 (₹30 crore) is more than ₹5 crore. Minimum spend = 2% of the average net profit of the 3 immediately preceding years.

| Particulars | ₹ crore |
| --- | --- |
| 2023-24 | 18 |
| 2024-25 | 24 |
| 2025-26 | 30 |
| Total | 72 |
| Average (72 / 3) | 24 |
| **2% of 24** | **0.48 = ₹48 lakh** |

questions.prompt: Does Indus Pharma need a CSR committee for FY 2026-27?
options: No, because the CSR obligation does not exceed ₹50 lakh; the Board discharges the committee's functions
Yes, every company to which section 135 applies needs a committee
No, because it is unlisted
Yes, because its turnover exceeds ₹200 crore
questions.explanation: Section 135(9): where the amount to be spent does not exceed ₹50 lakh, a CSR committee is not required and the Board discharges its functions. Indus must spend ₹48 lakh.

questions.prompt: Can AB and Co. be re-appointed as auditor at the AGM of 2026?
options: No, it has completed two terms of 5 consecutive years and must observe a 5-year cooling-off period
Yes, a firm can serve up to three terms
Yes, because rotation does not apply to unlisted companies
Yes, if the members pass a special resolution
questions.explanation: Indus is an unlisted public company with paid-up capital of ₹10 crore or more, so rotation applies under rule 5. Section 139(2)(b): an audit firm cannot be appointed for more than two terms of 5 consecutive years. AB and Co. has completed 2016-2021 and 2021-2026 and cannot be re-appointed for 5 years.

questions.prompt: Is CD and Associates disqualified because the partner's wife holds Indus shares of face value ₹80,000?
options: No, a relative may hold securities of face value up to ₹1 lakh
Yes, any holding by a relative disqualifies the firm
Yes, because the holding exceeds ₹50,000
No, because relatives are never considered
questions.explanation: Section 141(3)(d)(i) with rule 10: a relative of the auditor may hold securities of the company of face value not exceeding ₹1 lakh. ₹80,000 is within the limit. If it exceeded ₹1 lakh, corrective action would be required within 60 days.

questions.prompt: Is Indus Pharma required to appoint an internal auditor under section 138?
options: Yes, because it is an unlisted public company with paid-up capital of ₹50 crore or more and turnover of ₹200 crore or more
No, internal audit applies only to listed companies
No, because it has no deposits
Only if its statutory auditor recommends it
questions.explanation: Rule 13 makes internal audit compulsory for an unlisted public company with paid-up capital of ₹50 crore or more, or turnover of ₹200 crore or more, or borrowings of ₹100 crore or more, or deposits of ₹25 crore or more. Indus meets two tests.

questions.prompt: For how long must a company preserve its books of account under section 128?
options: At least 8 financial years immediately preceding the current year
5 years
10 years
Until the next statutory audit
questions.explanation: Section 128(5): books of account and vouchers are preserved in good order for at least eight financial years immediately preceding the financial year (longer if an investigation is ordered).

questions.prompt: The first auditor of a non-government company is appointed by:
options: The Board within 30 days of registration
The members at the first AGM
The Registrar within 60 days
The CAG within 60 days
questions.explanation: Section 139(6): the Board appoints the first auditor within 30 days of registration. If it fails, it informs the members, who appoint at an EGM within 90 days. The first auditor holds office till the first AGM.

questions.prompt: An auditor resigns mid-term. The Board fills the casual vacancy. What else is required?
options: Approval of members at a general meeting within 3 months of the Board's recommendation
Approval of the Central Government
Special notice from members
Nothing; the Board's appointment is final until the end of the original term
questions.explanation: Section 139(8): where the casual vacancy arises from resignation, the Board's appointment (made within 30 days) must also be approved at a general meeting convened within 3 months of the recommendation. The auditor holds office till the next AGM.

questions.prompt: The statutory auditor of a company may also carry out its internal audit if the Board approves.
questions.explanation: Section 144(b) prohibits the auditor from rendering internal audit services to the company, its holding or subsidiary company, directly or indirectly, whatever the Board decides.

questions.prompt: A company may voluntarily revise its financial statements for any of the three preceding financial years, with the approval of the Tribunal.
questions.explanation: Section 131(1): if the directors believe the statements do not comply with sections 129 or 134, they may revise them for any of the three preceding years after obtaining Tribunal approval, not more than once in a financial year.

questions.prompt: Which of these persons are disqualified from appointment as auditor of Orbit Ltd under section 141(3)? Select all that apply.
options: A CA who owes Orbit Ltd ₹6 lakh on a loan
A CA whose brother is the CFO of Orbit Ltd
A CA who is already the auditor of 20 companies
A CA whose mother holds Orbit Ltd shares of face value ₹60,000
An LLP of chartered accountants
questions.explanation: Indebtedness above ₹5 lakh, a relative who is a KMP (the CFO), and already auditing 20 companies are disqualifications. A relative may hold securities of face value up to ₹1 lakh, and an LLP is expressly allowed to be auditor.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: a person cannot be appointed auditor if he is already the auditor of more than ___ companies.
questions.explanation: Section 141(3)(g): a person in full-time employment elsewhere, or a person or partner who is already auditor of more than twenty companies, cannot be appointed.

questions.prompt: Explain the provisions relating to rotation of auditors under section 139(2) and rule 5 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014.
questions.answer:
Applicability (rule 5): listed companies; unlisted public companies with paid-up capital of ₹10 crore or more; private companies with paid-up capital of ₹50 crore or more; and all companies (not covered above) with public borrowings from financial institutions, banks or public deposits of ₹50 crore or more. OPCs and small companies are excluded.

Rules:
- An individual cannot be appointed or re-appointed for more than one term of 5 consecutive years.
- An audit firm cannot be appointed for more than two terms of 5 consecutive years.
- After completing the term, the individual or firm cannot be re-appointed for 5 years (cooling-off).
- During cooling-off, a firm having a common partner with the outgoing firm cannot be appointed.
- Members may further provide for rotation of the audit partner and team every year, or for joint audit.
- Existing companies were given a 3-year transition from the Act's commencement.

questions.prompt: Describe the procedure for removal of an auditor before the expiry of his term, and the provisions on resignation, under section 140.
questions.answer:
Removal (section 140(1), rule 7):
- Board resolution; application to the Central Government (Regional Director) in Form ADT-2 within 30 days of the Board resolution.
- The auditor is given a reasonable opportunity of being heard.
- After Central Government approval, a special resolution at a general meeting within 60 days of the approval.

Resignation (section 140(2) and (3)):
- The auditor files a statement in Form ADT-3 with the company and the Registrar within 30 days of resigning, giving reasons and other facts.
- Failure attracts a penalty of ₹50,000 or the auditor's remuneration, whichever is less, plus a daily penalty for continuing default (up to ₹5 lakh).

Special notice (section 140(4)) is needed to appoint a person other than the retiring auditor at an AGM. Under section 140(5) the Tribunal may order a change of auditor who acted fraudulently; such an auditor cannot be appointed by any company for 5 years.

questions.prompt: Decide with reasons: Mr Gupta, a chartered accountant, was appointed auditor of Neel Ltd at its AGM. Two months later he took a home loan of ₹7 lakh from Neel Ltd, which runs an employee and associate lending scheme. What is the effect on his appointment?
questions.answer:
Provision: section 141(3)(d)(ii) disqualifies a person who, or whose relative or partner, is indebted to the company, its subsidiary, holding or associate company, or their subsidiaries, in excess of ₹5 lakh. Section 141(4) states that if an auditor becomes subject to a disqualification after appointment, he shall vacate office and the vacancy is a casual vacancy.

Analysis: Mr Gupta's indebtedness of ₹7 lakh exceeds ₹5 lakh. The disqualification arose after his appointment.

Conclusion: Mr Gupta must vacate office as auditor of Neel Ltd. The Board fills the casual vacancy within 30 days under section 139(8).
