chapters.title: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
chapters.summary: Nature of an LLP, partners and designated partners, incorporation, liability, contribution, accounts and returns, conversion into LLP and winding up.
chapters.lawAsOf: Limited Liability Partnership Act 2008 as amended by the LLP (Amendment) Act 2021, and LLP Rules 2009 as amended up to November 2026. Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill 2026 (which also amends the LLP Act) not yet enacted.

lesson.heading: Nature of an LLP and comparison
lesson.body:
Section 3: an LLP is a body corporate formed and incorporated under the Act, a legal entity separate from its partners, with perpetual succession. A change in partners does not affect its existence, rights or liabilities. The Indian Partnership Act, 1932 does not apply to an LLP (section 4).

| Point | Partnership firm | LLP | Company |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Law | Indian Partnership Act, 1932 | LLP Act, 2008 | Companies Act, 2013 |
| Legal entity | Not separate from partners | Separate body corporate | Separate body corporate |
| Liability | Unlimited, joint and several | Limited to agreed contribution (except fraud) | Limited to unpaid amount on shares or guarantee |
| Members | 2 to 50 (as per rules) | Minimum 2, no maximum | Private 2-200, public 7 or more |
| Agency | Partner is agent of firm and of other partners | Partner is agent of the LLP only | Directors act for the company |
| Registration | Optional | Compulsory | Compulsory |
| Internal governance | Partnership deed | LLP agreement (First Schedule applies in its absence) | MOA and AOA |

Small LLP (section 2(1)(ta), inserted in 2021): contribution not more than ₹25 lakh (or a higher prescribed amount up to ₹5 crore) and turnover of the preceding financial year not more than ₹40 lakh (or a higher prescribed amount up to ₹50 crore). Both tests must be met. Small LLPs get lower penalties and simpler compliance.

lesson.heading: Partners, designated partners and incorporation
lesson.body:
- **Section 5**: any individual or body corporate may be a partner, except a person of unsound mind found so by a court, an undischarged insolvent, or a person who has applied to be adjudged insolvent with the application pending.
- **Section 6**: at least 2 partners. If the number falls below 2 and the LLP carries on business for more than 6 months, the person who is the only partner and knows it is personally liable for the LLP's obligations incurred during that period.
- **Section 7**: at least 2 designated partners who are individuals, and at least one of them resident in India. A resident is a person who has stayed in India for at least 120 days during the financial year (reduced from 182 days by the 2021 amendment). Where all partners are bodies corporate, their nominees act as designated partners. Each designated partner needs a DPIN or DIN and gives prior consent; particulars are filed within 30 days of appointment.
- **Section 8**: designated partners are responsible for compliance with the Act and liable to all penalties for contraventions.
- **Section 11**: for incorporation, two or more persons subscribe their names to an incorporation document, filed with the Registrar with a statement by an advocate, CA, CS or CMA engaged in the incorporation and by one of the subscribers. Under section 12 the certificate of incorporation is conclusive evidence of incorporation.
- **Section 15**: the name must end with "Limited Liability Partnership" or "LLP".
- **Section 23**: the LLP agreement and any change in it are filed with the Registrar (Form 3) within 30 days. Where there is no agreement on a matter, the First Schedule applies.
- **Sections 24 and 25**: a partner may cease by giving at least 30 days' notice to the other partners (subject to the agreement). The LLP files notice of any change in partners within 30 days (Form 4).

lesson.heading: Liability, contribution, accounts and returns
lesson.body:
- **Section 26**: every partner is an agent of the LLP, but not of the other partners.
- **Section 27**: the LLP is not bound by a partner's act where the partner had no authority and the other person knew it. The LLP is liable for a partner's wrongful act or omission in the course of its business or with its authority.
- **Section 28**: a partner is not personally liable for an obligation of the LLP solely because he is a partner; but he is personally liable for his own wrongful act or omission.
- **Section 30**: if an act is done with intent to defraud creditors or for any fraudulent purpose, the liability of the LLP and of the partners who acted with that intent is unlimited, and they are punishable.
- **Section 31**: courts and the Tribunal may reduce or waive penalties for a whistle-blowing partner or employee.
- **Section 32**: contribution may be tangible or intangible property, money, promissory notes, other agreements to contribute cash or property, or contracts for services. Its monetary value is accounted for and disclosed.

| Compliance | Section / rule | Due |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Books of account at registered office, preserved 8 years | 34 | Ongoing |
| Statement of Account and Solvency (Form 8) | 34 | Within 30 days from the end of 6 months of the financial year (by 30 October) |
| Audit of accounts | Rule 24(8) | Not compulsory if turnover does not exceed ₹40 lakh or contribution does not exceed ₹25 lakh in the year |
| Annual return (Form 11) | 35 | Within 60 days of the close of the financial year (by 30 May) |
| Accounting standards | 34A | As notified by the Central Government for classes of LLPs |

lesson.heading: Conversion, winding up and common mistakes
lesson.body:
| Conversion | Section and Schedule | Key conditions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Firm into LLP | 55, Second Schedule | All partners of the firm, and no one else, become partners of the LLP |
| Private company into LLP | 56, Third Schedule | No security interest subsisting or in force; all shareholders, and no one else, become partners |
| Unlisted public company into LLP | 57, Fourth Schedule | Same as for a private company |

Effects of conversion: all property, assets, interests, rights, privileges, liabilities and obligations of the firm or company transfer to and vest in the LLP without further assurance; the firm or company is deemed dissolved and removed from the records; pending proceedings continue by or against the LLP. The LLP informs the Registrar of Firms or Registrar of Companies within 15 days of the conversion.

Winding up (section 63, 64): voluntary, or by the Tribunal where the LLP so decides; partners fall below 2 for more than 6 months; it is unable to pay its debts; it acts against the sovereignty, integrity, security or public order of India; it fails to file the Statement of Account and Solvency or annual return for 5 consecutive financial years; or the Tribunal finds it just and equitable.

The 2021 amendment decriminalised many defaults, converting them into penalties adjudicated under section 76A, and introduced small LLPs, start-up LLPs, non-convertible debentures and the section 34A power to prescribe accounting standards.

**Common mistakes**: saying an LLP partner is agent of other partners; applying the 182-day residence test (now 120 days); confusing Form 8 (solvency, 30 October) with Form 11 (annual return, 30 May).

keyPoints: LLP is a body corporate with perpetual succession; Partnership Act 1932 does not apply (sections 3, 4).
Minimum 2 partners (section 6: sole partner liable after 6 months); at least 2 designated partners, one resident (120 days) (section 7).
Partner is agent of the LLP, not of other partners (26); not personally liable for LLP obligations except own wrongful act (28); unlimited liability in fraud (30).
Form 8 by 30 October; Form 11 within 60 days of FY end; audit not required if turnover up to ₹40 lakh or contribution up to ₹25 lakh.
Small LLP: contribution up to ₹25 lakh AND turnover up to ₹40 lakh (prescribable up to ₹5 crore / ₹50 crore).
Conversion: firm (Second Schedule), private company (Third), unlisted public company (Fourth).

cases.title: Case: Arya Designs LLP
cases.body:
Arya Designs LLP was incorporated in 2023. Its partners are Ms Anaya, Mr Bhaskar, Mr Dev and Zenith Interiors Private Limited (a body corporate).

| Particulars | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Designated partners | Ms Anaya and Mr Bhaskar |
| Days Ms Anaya stayed in India in FY 2025-26 | 130 |
| Days Mr Bhaskar stayed in India in FY 2025-26 | 60 |
| Total contribution | ₹20 lakh |
| Turnover for FY 2025-26 | ₹35 lakh |

In 2026, Mr Dev, acting within the LLP's business, made false promises to a client about material quality and caused a loss of ₹12 lakh to the client. Ms Anaya had no part in it. The client has sued the LLP, Mr Dev and Ms Anaya.

questions.prompt: Does Arya Designs LLP satisfy the requirement of a designated partner resident in India?
options: Yes, Ms Anaya stayed at least 120 days in the financial year
No, a resident must stay at least 182 days
No, both designated partners must be resident
Yes, because Zenith Interiors is an Indian company
questions.explanation: Section 7(1) explanation, as amended in 2021: a person resident in India is one who has stayed in India for at least 120 days during the financial year. Ms Anaya's 130 days qualifies, and only one designated partner needs to be resident.

questions.prompt: Is Arya Designs LLP a small LLP?
options: Yes, its contribution does not exceed ₹25 lakh and its turnover does not exceed ₹40 lakh
No, because a body corporate is one of its partners
No, because both tests must be below ₹10 lakh
Yes, but only because its turnover is below ₹40 lakh, whatever the contribution
questions.explanation: Section 2(1)(ta): a small LLP has contribution up to ₹25 lakh and turnover for the preceding financial year up to ₹40 lakh (or the higher amounts prescribed). Both conditions are met.

questions.prompt: Are Arya Designs LLP's accounts for FY 2025-26 required to be audited?
options: No, because turnover does not exceed ₹40 lakh (and contribution does not exceed ₹25 lakh)
Yes, every LLP must have its accounts audited
Yes, because a body corporate is a partner
No, but only if all partners pass a resolution
questions.explanation: Rule 24(8) of the LLP Rules exempts an LLP from audit where turnover does not exceed ₹40 lakh or contribution does not exceed ₹25 lakh in the financial year, unless the partners decide to have them audited.

questions.prompt: Who is liable to compensate the client for the ₹12 lakh loss caused by Mr Dev?
options: The LLP and Mr Dev; Ms Anaya is not personally liable
All partners jointly and severally, as in a partnership firm
Only Mr Dev; the LLP is not liable
Only Ms Anaya, as designated partner
questions.explanation: Section 27(2): the LLP is liable for a partner's wrongful act in the course of its business. Section 28(2): Mr Dev is personally liable for his own wrongful act. Section 28(1): Ms Anaya is not personally liable merely because she is a partner. If Mr Dev acted with intent to defraud, section 30 makes his liability (and the LLP's) unlimited.

questions.prompt: By what date must Arya file its Statement of Account and Solvency (Form 8) for FY 2025-26?
options: 30 October 2026
30 September 2026
31 March 2027
questions.explanation: Rule 24: the Statement of Account and Solvency is filed within 30 days from the end of six months of the financial year, that is by 30 October. The annual return (Form 11) is due within 60 days of the close of the year (30 May).

questions.prompt: What is the maximum number of partners an LLP can have?
options: No limit
questions.explanation: The LLP Act prescribes a minimum of 2 partners (section 6) but no maximum, unlike a partnership firm or a private company.

questions.prompt: An LLP must file its annual return within:
options: 60 days of the close of the financial year
30 days of the close of the financial year
6 months of the close of the financial year
30 days of its annual meeting
questions.explanation: Section 35(1): every LLP files an annual return with the Registrar within 60 days of the closure of its financial year, in Form 11.

questions.prompt: A body corporate that is a partner of an LLP can itself act as a designated partner.
questions.explanation: Section 7: designated partners must be individuals. A body corporate partner nominates an individual to act as designated partner.

questions.prompt: Every partner of an LLP is an agent of the other partners.
questions.explanation: Section 26: every partner is an agent of the LLP, but not of the other partners. This is a key difference from a partnership firm.

questions.prompt: Who cannot become a partner in an LLP under section 5? Select all that apply.
options: A person found to be of unsound mind by a competent court
An undischarged insolvent
A person who has applied to be adjudged insolvent and whose application is pending
A private limited company
A non-resident Indian individual
questions.explanation: Section 5 permits any individual or body corporate to be a partner, except the three categories listed. A company and a non-resident individual can be partners (at least one designated partner must be resident).

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: conversion of a private company into an LLP is governed by section 56 and the ___ Schedule to the LLP Act.
questions.explanation: Second Schedule: firm to LLP (section 55). Third Schedule: private company to LLP (section 56). Fourth Schedule: unlisted public company to LLP (section 57).

questions.prompt: Distinguish between a Limited Liability Partnership and a partnership firm.
questions.answer:
- Law: an LLP is governed by the LLP Act, 2008; a firm by the Indian Partnership Act, 1932.
- Legal status: an LLP is a body corporate with separate legal entity and perpetual succession (section 3); a firm is not separate from its partners.
- Liability: partners of an LLP are not personally liable for its obligations except for their own wrongful acts and fraud (sections 28, 30); partners of a firm have unlimited joint and several liability.
- Agency: an LLP partner is agent of the LLP only (section 26); a firm partner is agent of the firm and the other partners.
- Registration: compulsory for an LLP; optional for a firm.
- Number of partners: LLP minimum 2, no maximum; firm subject to a maximum prescribed under the Companies Act.
- Designated partners and statutory filings (Form 8, Form 11, audit) apply only to an LLP.
- Property: an LLP owns its property; a firm's property belongs to the partners jointly.

questions.prompt: Decide with reasons: Kiran and Mohan were the only partners of Sunrise Traders LLP. Mohan died on 1 April 2026. Kiran continued the business alone and in December 2026 bought goods worth ₹9 lakh on credit, which the LLP has not paid. The supplier sues Kiran personally. Decide.
questions.answer:
Provision: section 6(2) of the LLP Act. If at any time the number of partners is reduced below two and the LLP carries on business for more than six months while the number is so reduced, the person who is the only partner during the time it so carries on business after those six months, and has knowledge of it, is personally (severally) liable for the obligations of the LLP incurred during that period.

Analysis: the number of partners fell to one on 1 April 2026. The six-month period ended in early October 2026. The obligation of ₹9 lakh was incurred in December 2026, after six months. Kiran knew he was the only partner.

Conclusion: Kiran is personally liable for the ₹9 lakh owed to the supplier. The LLP is also open to winding up by the Tribunal under section 64.

questions.prompt: State the conditions and effects of conversion of a private company into an LLP under section 56 and the Third Schedule.
questions.answer:
Conditions:
- No security interest in the company's assets is subsisting or in force at the time of application.
- All the shareholders of the company, and no one else, become partners of the LLP.
- The company files the application with the Registrar with a statement of shareholders, the incorporation document and the required documents, including consent of all shareholders.

Effects (on registration):
- The company is converted into an LLP from the date of the certificate of registration.
- All tangible and intangible property, assets, interests, rights, privileges, liabilities and obligations of the company transfer to and vest in the LLP without further assurance.
- The company is deemed dissolved and removed from the records of the Registrar of Companies.
- Pending proceedings by or against the company continue by or against the LLP; existing agreements, contracts and employment continue.
- The LLP informs the Registrar of Companies within 15 days of the conversion.

questions.prompt: On what grounds can the Tribunal wind up an LLP under section 64?

chapters.title: Other Laws: General Clauses Act, Interpretation of Statutes and FEMA
chapters.summary: Key definitions and rules of the General Clauses Act 1897, the rules and aids of interpretation of statutes, and the Foreign Exchange Management Act 1999 framework for residents, current and capital account transactions and penalties.
chapters.lawAsOf: General Clauses Act 1897; Foreign Exchange Management Act 1999 and rules and RBI directions as amended up to November 2026 (LRS limit USD 2,50,000 per financial year).

lesson.heading: General Clauses Act, 1897
lesson.body:
The Act supplies common definitions and rules of construction so that every Central Act need not repeat them. Its definitions apply unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context.

| Section | Term or rule | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 3(13) | Commencement | The day on which the Act or Regulation comes into force |
| 3(22) | Good faith | A thing is done in good faith when it is in fact done honestly, whether done negligently or not |
| 3(26) | Immovable property | Includes land, benefits to arise out of land, and things attached to the earth or permanently fastened to anything attached to the earth |
| 3(35) | Month | A month reckoned according to the British calendar |
| 3(36) | Movable property | Property of every description, except immovable property |
| 3(42) | Person | Includes any company or association or body of individuals, whether incorporated or not |
| 3(66) | Year | A year reckoned according to the British calendar |
| 5 | Coming into operation | Where not otherwise expressed, a Central Act comes into operation on the day it receives the assent of the President, and operates from immediately on the expiry of the day preceding its commencement |
| 6 | Effect of repeal | Unless a different intention appears, repeal does not revive anything not in force, does not affect the previous operation of the repealed law, rights and liabilities acquired, penalties incurred, or pending investigations and proceedings |
| 9 | Commencement and termination of time | The word "from" excludes the first day of a period; the word "to" includes the last day |
| 10 | Office closed on last day | The act may be done on the next day the office is open (does not apply to the Limitation Act, 1963) |
| 13 | Gender and number | Words importing the masculine gender include females; the singular includes the plural and vice versa |
| 16 | Power to appoint | Includes power to suspend or dismiss |
| 21 | Power to issue notifications, orders, rules | Includes power to add to, amend, vary or rescind them |
| 26 | Offence under two enactments | The offender may be prosecuted under either, but shall not be punished twice for the same offence |
| 27 | Service by post | Deemed effected by properly addressing, pre-paying and posting by registered post, at the time the letter would be delivered in the ordinary course of post |

lesson.heading: Interpretation of statutes: rules
lesson.body:
| Rule | Meaning | When used |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Literal rule | Words are given their plain, ordinary and grammatical meaning | The primary rule, where words are clear |
| Mischief rule (Heydon's Case, 1584) | Ask: what was the law before, what mischief it did not cover, what remedy Parliament provided, and the true reason for the remedy; then suppress the mischief and advance the remedy | Where words are ambiguous and the purpose of the law is clear |
| Golden rule | Modify the literal meaning to the extent needed to avoid absurdity or inconsistency | Where the literal meaning leads to an absurd result |
| Harmonious construction | Read conflicting provisions of a statute so that each has effect | Where two provisions appear to conflict |
| Ejusdem generis | General words following specific words of a class are limited to things of the same class | Example: "cars, buses, trucks and other vehicles" does not cover aircraft |
| Noscitur a sociis | A word is known by the company it keeps | Ambiguous words read with their neighbours |
| Reddendo singula singulis | Words are applied distributively, each to its appropriate object | Lists of subjects and lists of actions |
| Strict construction | Penal and taxing statutes are read strictly; the benefit of doubt goes to the subject | Penal and fiscal laws |
| Beneficial construction | Welfare legislation is read liberally to advance its purpose | Labour and social welfare laws |

"Shall" usually indicates a mandatory provision and "may" a directory one, but the court looks at the scheme and purpose to decide.

lesson.heading: Interpretation of statutes: aids
lesson.body:
| Internal aids (within the statute) | External aids (outside the statute) |
| --- | --- |
| Long title and short title | Parliamentary history: statement of objects and reasons, debates, committee reports |
| Preamble | Historical facts and surrounding circumstances |
| Headings | Later social, political and economic developments and scientific inventions |
| Marginal notes | Dictionaries |
| Definition sections: "means" is exhaustive; "includes" is extensive | Earlier and later statutes in pari materia |
| Illustrations | Judicial decisions, including foreign decisions with caution |
| Proviso: carves out an exception from the main provision | Text books and commentaries |
| Explanation: clarifies the meaning of the main provision | |
| Schedules | |
| Punctuation (given limited weight) | |

A preamble or heading cannot override clear words of the enacting provisions; it helps only when the text is ambiguous.

lesson.heading: Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999
lesson.body:
FEMA consolidates the law on foreign exchange to facilitate external trade and payments and to promote orderly development of the foreign exchange market. It is a civil law: contraventions attract penalties, not imprisonment (except on failure to pay penalty).

Key definitions:

- **Authorised person (2(c))**: an authorised dealer, money changer, off-shore banking unit or other person authorised under section 10.
- **Capital account transaction (2(e))**: a transaction that alters the assets or liabilities, including contingent liabilities, outside India of persons resident in India, or in India of persons resident outside India.
- **Current account transaction (2(j))**: any transaction other than a capital account transaction, including payments for foreign trade and current business, short-term banking and credit facilities in the ordinary course, interest on loans and net income from investments, remittances for living expenses of parents, spouse and children abroad, and expenses for foreign travel, education and medical care of parents, spouse and children.
- **Person resident in India (2(v))**: a person residing in India for more than 182 days during the preceding financial year, but excluding (a) a person who has gone out of or stays outside India for employment, business or vocation outside India, or for any purpose indicating an intention to stay outside India for an uncertain period, and (b) a person who has come to or stays in India otherwise than for employment, business, vocation or a purpose indicating an intention to stay in India for an uncertain period. It also covers entities registered or incorporated in India, and offices, branches or agencies in India of persons resident outside India.

| Section | Provision |
| --- | --- |
| 3 | No dealing in foreign exchange or payments to non-residents except through an authorised person or as permitted |
| 4 | No person resident in India shall acquire, hold, own, possess or transfer foreign exchange or property outside India except as provided |
| 5 | Current account transactions are free, subject to reasonable restrictions by the Central Government (Current Account Transactions Rules: Schedule I prohibited, Schedule II needs Government approval, Schedule III limits; individuals can remit up to USD 2,50,000 per financial year under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme) |
| 6 | Capital account transactions only as permitted: RBI for debt instruments in consultation with the Government; the Central Government for non-debt instruments |
| 7, 8 | Exporters furnish declarations and realise and repatriate export proceeds within the specified period |
| 13 | Penalty up to three times the sum involved where quantifiable, or up to ₹2 lakh where not; further penalty up to ₹5,000 per day for continuing contravention |
| 15 | Compounding of contraventions within 180 days of application |
| 16-19 | Adjudicating authority, appeal to Special Director (Appeals), then to the Appellate Tribunal |

**Common mistakes**: treating a student or tourist who stays more than 182 days as resident; calling a purchase of property abroad a current account transaction; quoting imprisonment as the normal FEMA penalty.

keyPoints: GCA: 'from' excludes first day, 'to' includes last day (section 9); office closed on last day, next working day (section 10).
GCA: good faith = honestly, even if negligently (3(22)); person includes company and association (3(42)); Act operates from assent where no date given (5).
Repeal does not affect rights acquired, liabilities incurred or pending proceedings (GCA section 6).
Rules: literal, mischief (Heydon's Case), golden, harmonious, ejusdem generis, noscitur a sociis.
'Means' is exhaustive, 'includes' is extensive; proviso excepts, explanation clarifies.
FEMA resident: more than 182 days in preceding FY, excluding those leaving for employment and those coming for non-employment purposes (2(v)).
FEMA penalty: up to 3 times sum involved or ₹2 lakh; ₹5,000 a day continuing (13); LRS USD 2,50,000 per FY.

cases.title: Case: The Mehta family
cases.body:
- Mr Rohan Mehta lived in India for 200 days in FY 2025-26. On 15 June 2026 he left India to take up employment in Singapore for an uncertain period.
- His wife, Mrs Priya Mehta, who lives in Mumbai, remitted USD 2,70,000 during FY 2026-27 under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme to buy a flat in Dubai, without any other approval.
- An adjudicating authority found that a firm owned by Rohan's father had contravened FEMA in a transaction involving ₹40 lakh.
- Rohan's father received a show-cause notice requiring a reply "within 30 days from 1 October 2026".

questions.prompt: What is Mr Rohan Mehta's status under section 2(v) of FEMA from 15 June 2026?
options: Person resident outside India, because he has gone out of India for employment
Person resident in India, because he stayed more than 182 days in FY 2025-26
Person resident in India until 31 March 2027
Not covered by FEMA
questions.explanation: Section 2(v)(i)(A) excludes a person who has gone out of India or stays outside India for employment outside India, even if he stayed more than 182 days in the preceding year. Rohan became a person resident outside India from his departure for employment.

questions.prompt: Mrs Mehta's remittance of USD 2,70,000 to buy a flat in Dubai is:
options: A capital account transaction exceeding the LRS limit of USD 2,50,000 per financial year, needing specific approval
A current account transaction with no limit
Fully permitted under LRS, as there is no limit for property
Prohibited under Schedule I of the Current Account Transactions Rules
questions.explanation: Purchase of immovable property abroad alters assets outside India of a resident, so it is a capital account transaction (2(e)). An individual can remit up to USD 2,50,000 per financial year under LRS for permitted current and capital account transactions. The excess of USD 20,000 needs prior approval.

questions.prompt: The rule of interpretation laid down in Heydon's Case (1584) is the:
options: Mischief rule
Golden rule
Literal rule
Rule of harmonious construction
questions.explanation: Heydon's Case set out four questions: the law before the Act, the mischief not provided for, the remedy Parliament resolved, and the true reason for it. The court then interprets to suppress the mischief and advance the remedy.

questions.prompt: A statute says 'horses, cattle, sheep and other animals'. A court holds that 'other animals' does not include wild tigers. Which rule did it apply?
options: Ejusdem generis
Reddendo singula singulis
Golden rule
Beneficial construction
questions.explanation: Under ejusdem generis, general words following specific words of a distinct class (domestic or farm animals) are read as limited to things of the same class.

questions.explanation: 'Means' confines the term to the meaning given (exhaustive), while 'includes' enlarges the ordinary meaning (extensive). 'Means and includes' is also exhaustive.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: under FEMA, a person is resident in India if he resided in India for more than ___ days during the course of the preceding financial year (subject to exclusions).
questions.explanation: Section 2(v)(i): more than 182 days in the preceding financial year, excluding persons who left for employment or business abroad and persons who came to India for purposes other than employment, business or vocation.

questions.prompt: Explain the literal rule, the mischief rule, the golden rule and the rule of harmonious construction of interpretation.
questions.answer:
- Literal rule: the primary rule. Words are given their ordinary, natural and grammatical meaning. If the words are clear, the court applies them even if the result seems harsh; the remedy lies with the legislature.
- Mischief rule (Heydon's Case, 1584): the court considers the law before the Act, the mischief or defect it did not cover, the remedy Parliament provided and the reason for it, and interprets the provision to suppress the mischief and advance the remedy.
- Golden rule: a modification of the literal rule. Where the literal meaning leads to absurdity, inconsistency or hardship, the court modifies the words to the extent needed to avoid it, but no further.
- Harmonious construction: where two provisions of the same statute appear to conflict, the court construes them so that both are given effect. One provision should not be read so as to render the other useless.

questions.prompt: Explain the effect of repeal of an enactment under section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897.

Decide with reasons: Mr James, a UK citizen, came to India as a tourist and then enrolled in a two-year course at a Pune university. He stayed in India for 250 days in FY 2025-26 and continues to study in FY 2026-27. Is he a person resident in India under FEMA for FY 2026-27?
questions.answer:
Provision: section 2(v)(i) of FEMA. A person residing in India for more than 182 days in the preceding financial year is resident, but sub-clause (B) excludes a person who has come to or stays in India, in either case, otherwise than for or on taking up employment, carrying on business or vocation in India, or for any other purpose indicating an intention to stay in India for an uncertain period.

Analysis: Mr James stayed 250 days in FY 2025-26, which exceeds 182 days. But he came as a tourist and stays for a course of study of a definite duration. These purposes are not employment, business or vocation, and do not show an intention to stay for an uncertain period.

Conclusion: Mr James is not a person resident in India under FEMA for FY 2026-27; he remains a person resident outside India despite staying more than 182 days.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between current account transactions and capital account transactions under FEMA, with the regulatory approach to each.
questions.answer:
- Definition: a capital account transaction (2(e)) alters the assets or liabilities, including contingent liabilities, outside India of persons resident in India, or in India of persons resident outside India. A current account transaction (2(j)) is any transaction other than a capital account transaction.
- Examples: capital - investment in foreign shares, property abroad, external commercial borrowings, guarantees. Current - trade payments, interest and investment income, travel, education and medical expenses, maintenance of close relatives abroad.
- Regulation: current account transactions are freely permitted (section 5), subject to reasonable restrictions by the Central Government through the Current Account Transactions Rules (Schedule I prohibited, Schedule II with Government approval, Schedule III with limits).
- Capital account transactions are permitted only to the extent specified (section 6): by RBI for debt instruments in consultation with the Central Government, and by the Central Government for non-debt instruments.
- Both must be done through authorised persons (section 3, 10). Individuals may use LRS up to USD 2,50,000 per financial year for permitted transactions of either kind.
